en: Then, in the dust mandala or within another mandala, having first performed the preliminary rites—such as the consecration of the vase (*kalaśādhivāsana*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*) according to the previously stated procedure—one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciples. These disciples must be well-tested, free from defects such as pride (*māna*) and the like, refined by their training in the vows of the lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) and so forth, and devoted. Even those lacking noble lineage, good qualities, or beauty may be consecrated if they are fit to receive the *vajrasattva* vows (*saṃvara*). This applies provided that, out of faith, they are intensely desirous of the *vajrasattva* vows and have no other teacher than the Vajrayāna.

Then, whether it be in a mandala of colored powders or any other mandala, having first performed the ritual as previously described—including the preliminary consecration of the vase (*kalaśādhivāsana*), its placement, and the five types of offerings such as those of service—one should [admit] disciples who have been thoroughly examined and are free from defects such as pride.

Those who have fully attained the training of the lay devotee (*upāsaka*) and so forth, who are thoroughly purified and endowed with reverence, and who possess the capacity to maintain the meditation on Vajrasattva—even those lacking the qualities of noble lineage or physical beauty—should be established as superior residents.
If they too, through faith, should intensely seek the meditation on Vajrasattva and not search for another teacher in the Vajrayāna; |||
This was stated by the Blessed One in the *Sārdhatriśatikā*:
"One should tolerate those who are deformed, devoid of qualities, or even inferior;
the ritual for the mandala is authorized for all four types of assemblies."
"For those who are engaged in their own trainings and whose minds delight in the Mahāyāna."

"Of the four assemblies" refers to monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. "The procedure" refers to the rites of entry and so forth. "Of those who are disciplined and devoted to it" means those whose very selves delight in the Mahāyāna. By this, he demonstrates that mental action is the primary factor of this vehicle, for the sake of showing its non-contradiction [with other teachings].

This was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Three Hundred and Fifty [Stanzas]*: "One should dwell even more [reverently] toward those who are ugly, devoid of qualities, or inferior; likewise, one should grant the ritual permissions for mandalas to the fourfold assembly. Those who are well-endowed with their respective trainings and possess the intention that delights in the Mahāyāna. The "fourfold assembly" refers to the bhikṣus and [the other three groups].

[The recipients are] bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. The ritual consists of the introduction and so forth. "Endowed" means being diligent. By this [phrase], "one whose intention delights in the Mahāyāna," it is shown that mental activity is primary in this vehicle; this is for the purpose of avoiding contradictions.

For even regarding an action that is naturally reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*), the Blessed One has frequently declared that there is no transgression due to a particularity in the motivation (*samutthāna*). And so it was declared:
"The Caṇḍālas, bamboo-workers, and others who contemplate their purpose for the sake of death..."
They too, having relied upon Hevajra, attain accomplishment; there is no doubt in this matter.
Furthermore, in the path of Hevajra,
there is no transgression for one who possesses a virtuous mind and is motivated by affection and compassion.
"Even that which is forbidden is permitted for the compassionate one who perceives the welfare [of others]."

The Blessed One has extensively taught that even for those who perform actions inherently blameworthy, there are many instances where they do not fall [into lower realms] due to the distinction of their motivation (*āśaya*). Thus it is said: "Even outcastes, fowlers, and the like, who intend to kill for the sake of profit—if they know Hevajra, they will attain accomplishment; of this there is no doubt. And elsewhere:

"There is no downfall for one whose mind is virtuous, because they possess compassion and love," and as it is said: "For one who possesses compassion and perceives the ultimate purpose, even that which is prohibited is permitted."

Furthermore, for one who has accumulated merit and extensive learning (*bāhuśrutya*) and so forth, and who possesses firm conviction that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams and have the single flavor of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), how could there even be a scent of contradiction between the vows of a monk and those of a Vajradhara? For this very reason, the Blessed One stated, "One should make a monk a Vajradhara," and this must necessarily be accepted.

Otherwise, how could it be reconciled with what is established in the Vinaya— that a monk who, due to the simultaneous awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of both, sees a dream and experiences pleasure while a woman outside [the monastery] is likewise seeing the dream and experiencing pleasure up to the culmination of the pleasure of the two organs, remains free from offense? This must be explained.

[The one] who has repeatedly accumulated much merit, such as extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) and so forth, and who possesses an extremely firm conviction that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams and are of one taste in emptiness— for such a person practicing the meditation of the Vajradhara Bhikṣu, how could there be even a trace of the stain of contradiction? For this very reason, the Blessed One said:
It is said: "The monk named Vajradhara. This must certainly be accepted; otherwise, how could both exist simultaneously?

One should understand the teaching of the Vinaya as follows: if a monk, due to the awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), sees in a dream the pleasure associated with that experience of bliss he has felt, and even if he experiences the ultimate pleasure of the two external organs [of union] seen in that dream, there is no offense. Thus is the Vinaya to be understood.

If, however, the location should be a domain frequented by wicked people, then even for such a person the secret and wisdom-knowledge empowerments (*guhya-prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka*) should be bestowed using the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*). But in the absence of wicked people, they should be bestowed by means of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) alone. However, for a monk whose conviction regarding reality is not firm, even if he is faithful, the reception of empowerment through an external wisdom-consort (*bāhyaprajñā*) is forbidden; otherwise, due to the loss of his previous vows, there would be great harm. [Note: *adṛḍhatattvādhimokṣasya* is repeated in the source.]

If, moreover, he should be shown to have a sphere of activity involving base births, then at that time, the seal of gnosis (*jñānamudrā*) and the empowerment of the wisdom-gnosis (*prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka*) should be bestowed upon him; however, if there are no base persons present, it should be done by means of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) itself.

For a monk whose conviction regarding suchness is unstable, even if he possesses faith, his taking of the outer consort is forbidden; otherwise, by violating his previous vows, it would result in a great futility.

If, however, the guru is one whose realization is stable, then when the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā) is offered by him, the wisdom-consecration (prajñābhiṣeka) should also be bestowed upon him; and for the recipient, there is not even a suspicion of non-celibacy, because of the absence of physical action. For him, however, the distinctions of joy and so forth are to be demonstrated through the recollection of the bliss experienced previously during his state as a householder.

Furthermore, if one has become stable in the meditation on the guru, then at that time, one should also bestow upon him the empowerment of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) by means of the wisdom-mudrā (*jñānamudrā*) entrusted by him. Regarding its reception, there is no fear of being separated from celibacy (*brahmacarya*), because there is no physical action involved.
Furthermore, if one previously lived as a householder, one should bring to mind the pleasures experienced therein and firmly stabilize the various distinctions such as joy and so forth.
Even if the guru is a monk, all that has been said regarding the bestowing of the secret initiation and so forth should be applied here as well.
When the guru has become a bhikṣu, then upon bestowing the secret empowerment, the initiation, and so forth, one should perform the connection [of the ritual] by reciting everything.
Thus, enough of this digression; the subject at hand is now discussed.
Enough with excessive elaboration; we shall now discuss the matter at hand.

Thereafter, for the disciples who have prepared the maṇḍala, taken handfuls of flowers, and placed their knees upon the ground—those who are fit for the way of Mantra—the entry into the maṇḍala should be performed not merely for the sake of prosperity in this world, nor even for prosperity in the next world, but rather for the attainment of the perfection of the three bodies (trikāya) of the Tathāgata.

Having thus proclaimed that "in this way, the two types of prosperity will be accomplished," he should mentally cause those disciples to enter his own body through his mouth. Having visualized them as emerging from his own vajra and seated upon lotuses of the vidyā-mantras appearing within himself, and having been consecrated by the Tathāgatas together with their vidyās—who have entered through his mouth and melted—drawn in by rays from the seed-syllable in his heart; then, having seated them at the eastern gate of the maṇḍala, he should have them request entry.
[The text reads: *tathāgatakāya* and *svapratibhāni*.

Following that, the disciples should construct a maṇḍala and, with palms joined holding flowers and their right knees touching the ground, [the teacher should address] those who are fortunate enough to possess the capacity for the way of mantra: "It is not for the sake of seeking high status in this very world, nor even for the sake of high status in the next world."

"Furthermore, one should enter the mandala in order to attain the excellence of the three bodies of the Tathāgata. By doing so, one will also attain the two types of higher rebirth. Having proclaimed this, he drew the disciples into his own body through his mouth.

Visualize that those [deities] who reside within the lotuses of the wisdom-consorts—emerging from one's own vajra path and abiding in their own radiance—are summoned by light rays from the seed-syllable at the heart; the Tathāgatas together with their wisdom-consorts enter through the mouths [of the deities], melt, and confer the empowerment. Then, having placed them at the eastern gate of the mandala, have them offer a prayer for entry.
O Great Hero, you alone are my Teacher and the sole deliverer from the ocean of existence, which is terrifying with its crocodiles of death, birth, old age, and disease.
O Great Lord, I, who am greatly devoted, desire the firm path of great awakening; grant me the commitment (*samaya*),
grant me the reality (*tattva*), and grant me the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
O Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, grant me the three refuges;
[I take] refuge.
O Lord, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation.

“From the ocean of existence, which is terrifying with its crocodiles and other [beasts] such as birth, aging, and death, please liberate me! O Teacher of Great Joy, you alone have shown the way to great enlightenment; I seek you, the Great Protector! Grant me the reality of the samaya; grant me also the bodhicitta! [Grant me] the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha!”
Grant me also the three refuges; O Protector, please lead me into the city of great liberation.
Having thus recited [the text], and then having made one disciple the principal [figure]:
"Come, child, to this method of the practice of mantra in the Mahāyāna."
I shall teach you correctly, for you are a worthy vessel for the Great Way.
The Buddhas, arisen throughout the three times, who possess the vajras of body, speech, and mind,
have attained incomparable gnosis through the cultivation of vajra mantras.
By means of this incomparable application of mantra,
the exceedingly terrible and mighty army of Māra was shattered by the excellent ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas.
Having followed the ways of the world by means of their powers and having set the wheel in motion, they have attained final liberation.
Therefore, my child, apply this mind toward the attainment of omniscience.

Come here, you! This is the Great Vehicle. I shall perfectly teach to you the rituals of the way of Secret Mantra practice. You are a vessel for the great way; by means of the power of the Vajra Mantra, the Buddhas who appear in the three times have perfectly attained incomparable primordial wisdom. The application of Secret Mantra is indeed peerless.

"By whom the Śākya lion and others—those supreme ones—overcame the great and fierce hosts of Māra; who, having understood how to follow the world, turned the wheel [of Dharma] and passed into parinirvāṇa—for that reason, my son, apply this intelligence in order to attain omniscience.
Having thus recited it himself, he then said: "Thus [it is]."
I take refuge in the Three Jewels; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; I set my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.
I take refuge in the Three Jewels; I individually confess all my sins; I rejoice in the virtue of beings; I mentally embrace the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Thus, one should have him recite it three times.
Thus, in order for one who possesses the common vows to receive the vows of an ācārya:
"O Lord, having bestowed the irreversible consecration upon the wheel, please speak to me."
The reality of the wheel and its deity, and the ritual service for the preceptor.
I shall eternally be the preceptor of the supreme secret vow, the commitment of all Buddhas, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings.

"O Protector, please bestow upon me, your servant, the supreme empowerment of the irreversible wheel. Please explain the reality of the deity of the wheel, the ritual activities of the preceptor, the samaya of all the Buddhas, and the supreme secret vow. For the sake of the benefit of all sentient beings, may I always serve as a preceptor."
Having thus caused [the disciple] to make this specific request, one should cause them to generate the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Having been thus specially exhorted to pray, one should generate the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) as follows:
"May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attend to me! May the Preceptor attend to me! From this moment until I sit upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I, named so-and-so..."

May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas turn their attention toward me! May the Master turn his attention toward me! I, who am called [name], from this time forth until I reach the heart of enlightenment, generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening, just as the Protectors of the three times have resolved upon perfect awakening.
I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline, the gathering of wholesome qualities, and the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha with respect to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— the supreme and unsurpassed Three Jewels.
I truly accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā;
and I shall accept the master in the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the four gifts six times every day:
material goods, fearlessness, the true Dharma, and loving-kindness, for the sake of the exaltation of the Buddha-family.
In the great Jewel Family, which is worthy and delightful in its timing,
I accept the True Dharma— outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles.
In the pure Mahāpadma family, which originates from great awakening,
I accept from all sides the vow associated with everything.
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed bodhicitta, one should perform the rite of worship according to one's ability within the exalted assembly of the Mahākarmakula.
Having taken up the complete vow for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings,
I shall ferry across those who have not crossed over, and I shall liberate those who are not yet liberated.
I shall bring comfort to beings who have not found comfort; I shall establish them in nirvāṇa.

Just as the Protectors of the three times have resolved upon awakening, I shall generate the unsurpassed, sublime mind of awakening (bodhicitta). I shall firmly and individually uphold the three types of ethical discipline: the discipline of training, the discipline of gathering virtuous qualities, and the discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings. [I take refuge in] the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

From this day forth, I shall firmly uphold the vows born from the yoga of the Buddha—the unsurpassed Triple Gem. I shall also properly take up the vajra, the jewel, the bell, and the mudrā; I shall likewise accept the masters. And regarding the delightful commitments of the great and supreme Jewel Family:

Every day, at each of the six times, one should bestow the four kinds of gifts individually. Within the pure and great Lotus Family, which arises from Great Enlightenment, one should individually uphold the sublime Dharma of the three vehicles—outer, secret, and inner. Within the supreme gathering of the Karma Family, being perfectly endowed with all vows, one should individually uphold that very reality.

I shall perform acts of worship to the best of my ability. For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I shall generate the unsurpassed, sublime, and perfect bodhicitta; having taken up the vows in their entirety, I shall ferry across those who have not crossed over, I shall liberate those who are not liberated, I shall bring breath to those who have not found breath, and I shall establish sentient beings in nirvāṇa.
Having thus caused [the disciple] to recite it three times.
Thus he was made to recite this three times.

Thereafter, having protected them with the *Amṛtakuṇḍali* mantra and visualized the syllables *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*—black, red, and white respectively—resting upon a sun, a sun-and-moon disk, and a moon situated atop a vajra, lotus, and wheel at their heart, throat, and head; and while reciting those syllables, having touched the heart, throat, and head with the right fist holding a vajra moistened with scented water, one should offer a flower on the head, incense and a lamp before [the face], and again scent at the heart.

Following that, having protected [them] with the Amṛtakuṇḍalī mantra, one should visualize upon their hearts, throats, and crowns the syllables HŪṂ, ĀḤ, and OṂ—black, red, and white respectively—resting upon sun, lotus, and moon discs atop vajras, lotuses, and wheels.

Then, while reciting [the mantra], one should touch the heart, the throat, and the crown of the head with scented water together with the vajra; thereafter, one should offer flowers upon the head, incense, lamps, and once again, scent, at the heart.

Then, he should give to the disciples a tooth-stick made of *aśvattha* or other suitable wood, twelve finger-breadths long, straight, free of insects, unsplit, without blemishes, washed with fragrant water, and with a flower tied to its tip. They, facing either east or north within a four-cubit square mandala smeared with cow dung and the like, recite "Oṃ vajrahāsa haṃ" and, having chewed it from the tip until it is split, they cast it away without regard, looking upward as it falls directly before them.

One should declare their future success according to the direction in which their tooth-sticks fall: by falling toward the east, north, west, south, upward, downward, or face-down, there are respectively the attainments of pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśya*), malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the state of a *vidyādhara*, and the underworld (*pātāla*). However, if they fall outside the mandala, there is no success.

Thereafter, having given them water consecrated with the syllable *vaṃ* for rinsing the mouth, or else three handfuls of scented water consecrated seven times with the *kuṇḍalinī* mantra while reciting: "Oṃ hrīḥ! O Pure Dharma, purify all the sins of this person; remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ!"—one should cause them to drink it.

Then, having seated them outside, one should give many *kuśa* grasses with unbroken tips—either consecrated with the *hūṃjā* or the *kuṇḍalijā* mantra—for the purpose of spreading as a seat, with the mantra: *Oṃ vajratīkṣṇa vaṃ*.

With the mantra *āḥ śvadhā* and so forth, he gives to the disciples tooth-sticks that are twelve finger-widths long, straight, free of living organisms, undecayed, without blemishes, moistened with fragrant water, and with flowers tied to their tips; these disciples then [use] the tooth-sticks while facing east or north upon a mandala measuring four cubits and smeared with cow dung and the like.

Having recited "oṃ vajra hāsa haṃ," one should bite off the tip; then, looking upward without hesitation, it should be cast forward. Following the direction in which the tooth-stick falls among those [deities], the siddhi that will arise should be proclaimed.

If [the mark] points toward the east, north, west, south, above, or below, there will be, respectively, the accomplishments of pacification, enrichment, magnetizing, wrathful activity, the state of a vidyādhara, and the subterranean accomplishments. If it falls beyond the perimeter of the maṇḍala, there is no accomplishment.

Following that, having given water produced from the syllable *baṃ* for the purpose of rinsing the mouth, one should cause [the disciple] to drink while reciting three handfuls of scented water over which the *saptāvarta* mantra has been recited, saying: *oṃ hrīḥ viśuddha sarvadharmāḥ sarvapāpaṃ me tasya śodhaya sarvavikalpān āpanayya hūṃ*.

Then, having placed them outside, one should give *kuśa* grass for the purpose of a pillow—grass produced from the syllable *hūṃ* and recited with that [mantra] or wound around it—by uttering the mantra: *oṃ vajratīkṣṇa vaṃ*.

Thereafter, having taken a thread spun by a virgin, equal in length to the body of the disciple, tripled, and tied with three knots while reciting the Amṛtakuṇḍalī mantra, he himself should bind it upon their right arm—or the left for women—while reciting "Oṃ buddhamaitrī rakṣa 2 sarvān svāhā," and thus providing perfect protection, he should inspire them with enthusiasm.

Following that, one should take a thread spun by a young girl, measure it to the length of one's own body, and tie three knots while reciting the *Amṛtakuṇḍalī* mantra. Then, while reciting "Oṃ buddhame tri rakṣa rakṣa sarvān svāhā," one should bind it oneself upon the right upper arm for a man or the left for a woman, thereby providing perfect protection and generating joy.
[One should reflect: "Whatever evil was committed in the past over many millions of eons..."
For all that indeed goes to destruction upon seeing such a mandala.
The occurrence of all suffering, which is the source of miserable rebirths,
is destroyed for those whose minds are utterly pure regarding this supreme conduct.
Today, O great-souled ones, you have obtained incomparable gains,
in that you have been admitted here into the teaching of all the Victors together with their sons.
All of you have been taken up by great beings as soon as you were born;
therefore, you shall indeed be well-born in the Mahāyāna.
This is the glorious, supreme path, the great success of the Mahāyāna,
by which you, proceeding along it, shall become Tathāgatas.

Whatever sins were committed in the past throughout many tens of millions of eons, all of them will be exhausted by seeing a maṇḍala such as this. For those whose intellects are utterly stainless regarding this supreme practice, all their sufferings and the lower realms from which they arise will be completely pacified. By you, O great beings—

Today you have obtained an incomparable gain! By that through which you have all been fully embraced within this teaching of the Victors and their great-souled Sons, you will truly be born into the Mahāyāna. This supreme path, from which the Great Vehicle so greatly arises, is endowed with glory.
Whoever shall go forth [from this world] will become a Tathāgata.

Having thus caused them to hear this, and having subsequently protected them with the Kuṇḍalī mantra, he should explain the Kuṇḍalī mantra for the purpose of their recitation, saying: "Whatever dream you see, you shall relate it all to me in the morning. Having spoken thus, he should have them sleep inside the maṇḍala house behind a curtain, or elsewhere on a lion’s bed. He himself, having entered the maṇḍala house, should recite the Kuṇḍalī mantra for the sake of protection. (1) *omit* \ed; *yavanikādyantarite* \ed (and Tib.!!!)

Having thus caused them to listen, he then protected them with the *āvarta-mantra* and had them recite the *āvarta-mantra* for the purpose of the recitation. Having commanded them, saying, "Whatever you see even slightly in your dreams, report all of that to me in the morning," he should have them lie down in the lion’s posture, either inside the maṇḍala house, or within a partitioned area such as a curtain, or elsewhere as appropriate.

In this context, the vow (*saṃvara*) that is bestowed even without making someone an *ācārya* is the "general" one, characterized merely by taking refuge and generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). However, that which is bestowed for the purpose of making someone an *ācārya* is the "ācārya-vow," which is comprised of the five families. Therefore, this is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciple, preceded by the bestowing of these two vows.

The disciple’s own residence: Having entered the mandala palace oneself as well, one should recite the *āvartana* mantra for the purpose of protection. Here, that which is granted even to those who do not act as preceptors, but merely practice meditation, is the common [rite], characterized simply by taking refuge and generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Furthermore, that which is bestowed upon one who acts as a preceptor is the preceptor’s vow (*ācāryasaṃvara*), which is comprised of five classes. Therefore, this is the ritual for the formal residence of a disciple, preceded by the bestowal of these two vows.

Thereafter, at dawn, the Guru, having offered the *bali* and emerged from the maṇḍala house, asks the disciples about their dreams. If an inauspicious dream is indicated by such signs as falling from a mountain, he protects them with the *kuṇḍalī* mantra. Then, at the time of re-entering the maṇḍala house, being encouraged by the disciples with the words: "Oṃ, enter, O Blessed One, into the city of liberation of great bliss, which bestows the bliss of all accomplishments! O supreme, most excellent Great Bliss, be accomplished! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ, may you be fully accomplished!"—thus being encouraged.

Following that, the preceptor offers the *bali* in the morning and emerges from the mandala house. He should then inquire about the dreams of the disciples; any inauspicious dreams indicated by such signs as falling from a mountain and so forth should be protected against with the *āvartana-mantra*.

Furthermore, at the time of re-entering the mandala house, the disciples should be inspired with [the following] mantra: *oṃ braviṣa bhagavān mahāsukhamokṣasuraṃ sarvabuddhapradaṃ paramasukhotpādasiddhyai jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ prasiddhya svāhā*. Thus they should be thoroughly inspired.
Then, having emerged from that state, the Lord of Yogins, radiant with wide-open eyes,
should circumambulate the wheel and begin the opening of the door.
Standing at the western gate, vibrating with the pratyālīḍha stance,
one should first recite [the mantra] and remove the door with the Vajra-hūṃkāra mudrā.
Oṃ, Vajra, open! Enter the samaya! Hūṃ.
At that time, standing thus in the northern direction and reciting with a wrathful gaze,
he should open the southern door and release the wrathful mudrā.
The yogi, stationed in the eastern direction and likewise facing westward,
shall open the western gate and release the krodhamudrā.
Likewise, situated in the southern direction, proceeding clockwise as before,
one should open the door presided over by Dhanada and enter again in this manner.

Then, having risen, the Lord of Yogins, with eyes blazing and fully expanded, circumambulates to the right and shall shatter the Māras by opening the gates of the wheel. Abiding at the western gate, with the left leg extended in a posture of valor, he speaks these words in order to open the eastern gate and performs the mudrā of Vajra-hūṃ-kāra.

oṃ vajra-dgah-tsa-sa-ma-ya-bra-be-sha-ya hūṃ | Likewise, remaining correctly in the north, one speaks thus with a wrathful gaze; the southern gate is to be opened, and liberation is to be performed through the wrathful mudrā. Remaining correctly in the eastern direction, likewise the yogin faces the west; the watery gate is to be opened, and liberation is to be performed through the wrathful mudrā.
Likewise, one should correctly abide in the southern direction; by circling to the right as before, one should open the gate where Vaiśravaṇa dwells, and in that manner, one should enter once again.

Having cast a flower garland into the maṇḍala with the mantra: *oṃ paramasukhāśayasulalitavilāsanamitair namāmi bhagavantaṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ hi hi hi hi hīḥ pratīccha kusumāñjaliṃ nātha hor*, and having taken it up again and bound it upon one's own head with the intention of receiving the garland empowerment (*mālābhiṣeka*), one should visualize the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*) and the Guru as being manifest before one. Then, one should receive all the empowerments—beginning with the garland empowerment—that are being bestowed by him, according to the ritual procedure as will be described hereafter.

Having obtained permission for all the master’s rites, one should desire the accomplishment of the mandala for the entry of the disciple— preceded by a praise of the reality of wisdom and means whose nature is great bliss— and should perform the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
And [one should visualize] the wheel consisting of wisdom and means.

Having cast [the flower] into the mandala with the mantra: *oṃ paraṃ sukhaśaya sulalita vilāsane | mitte | namaḥ bhagavantaṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ hi hi hi hi hiḥ pratīccha kusumāñjali nātha hoḥ*, one should then take it back up and bind it to the head with the intention of conferring the garland initiation (*mālā-abhiṣeka*).

One should have intense conviction that the Lord of the Mandala (cakreśvara) is present before one’s very eyes as the Guru; from him, one should receive all the empowerments—beginning with the holding of the garland empowerment—that are about to be explained, as well as the authorization for all the activities of a master (ācāryakarma) according to the ritual procedure, in order to initiate the disciples.

Preceded by a praise of reality (*tattva*), which is the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) consisting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*), one should request the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the maṇḍala and perform the consecration of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*):
Because its sign is born from space, it is supreme, without beginning or end. (The reading *anādhinidhanaḥ* is preferred over *anādinidhanaḥ*.)
O Being composed of the great vajra, O Akṣobhyavajra and others, grant me accomplishment!
O Sovereign of all supreme great siddhis, presiding deity of sovereignty,
King who holds all vajras, may you grant me the realization of the supreme syllable.
You are the supreme syllable,
faultless and eternal,
the one who inspires passion for all that is passionate.
O Blessed One, through reality, may great passion and great delight be accomplished for me.
The Great Joy,
the supreme dharma of ultimate purity, the Tathāgata liberated from the beginning;
the Tathāgata.
O Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva who is the self of all, grant me success!
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra [attains] the supreme great siddhi through the mudrā of the pinnacle of sovereignty.
O Vajragarvāpati, through the great excellence of the perfected Vajra, may [this] be mine.
Pervading the minds of all sentient beings,
he dwells within the hearts of all sentient beings.
He is indeed the father of all sentient beings, and the foremost among those who hold the supreme samaya of desire.
By that truth through which my gnosis is the maṇḍala consisting of wisdom and skillful means,
by that truth, O Lord, fulfill my desires!
Phenomena are like reflections: transparent, pure, and unclouded;
they are ungraspable and inexpressible, yet they arise from causes and karma.

"By the truth that [the mandala] has emerged from the reality of suchness (tathatātattva), may all stainless disciples behold the mandala clearly as a reflection. Reciting this, he should perform the empowerment through truth (satyādhiṣṭhāna). This is the entry of the master.

Because space is characterized by arising, it is the supreme [state] without beginning or end. O Great Vajrasattva, whose nature is such, may I today be established as Akṣobhyavajra! You are the great sovereign, the supreme deity, the king of all Vajradharas, the great siddhi that is the pinnacle of all. O faultless and eternal one, please establish me in the supreme immutability!

Following after all forms of passion, the great passion, the great joy—O Blessed One, may you establish me in that very reality! May you establish me as the Bodhisattva, the supreme Dharma utterly pure, primordially liberated, the Tathāgata, Samantabhadra, the self-nature of all! Possessing the mudrā of supreme sovereignty, the most excellent of all great siddhis!

O Great Vajra of Accomplishment, clearly manifest! Grant me the accomplishment of the pride of the vajra! Pervading the minds of all sentient beings, you dwell in the hearts of all sentient beings; you are the father of all sentient beings as well, the supreme samaya of the highest desire. By that truth of the mandala whose nature is wisdom and method, O Protector, may you completely fulfill my desires!

"All phenomena are like reflections—luminous, pure, and untroubled; they cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed, yet they arise perfectly from causes and karma. By this truth, may all disciples behold the mandala clearly as a reflection, free from obscuration. Having spoken thus, this is the entry of the master.

Then, the disciple—who has undergone the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), who observes the two vows, who stands behind a curtain at the eastern door, and who has been purified with fragrant substances and the like—is visualized in the form of Vairocana or as the Lord of the Wheel. He is clothed in red garments or other [colored] robes with the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānuttarabodhyalaṃkāravastrapūjāmeghasamudraspharaṇasamaye hūṃ*. He wears an upper garment (*uttarīya*) with the mantra: *oṃ vajrarakṣa haṃ*, and [the head-protection] with: *oṃ vajroṣṇīṣa hūṃ phaṭ*.

Having donned the turban, having had the blindfold bound with the mantra *oṃ cakṣurbandhaṃ varam ānaya hūṃ*, having taken up a garland of flowers with *āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ*, and having been sprinkled with water from the all-purpose flask after offering the ritual fee, [the disciple] is led by a Yoginī or by the Karmavajrī who holds him.
Having placed [him], [he is made to stand].
The blindfold is bound.
Then,

having performed the consecration (*adhivāsana*) with water offerings and established the disciple— who possesses the two vows— at the eastern gate partitioned by a curtain, one should visualize him as the form of Vairocana or as the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*), having been purified with fragrant substances and the like.

With the mantra *oṃ sarvatathāgatānuttarabodhyalaṅkāravastropūjāmeghasamayaspharaṇa hūṃ*, one should wear a lower garment of red cloth or any other suitable material; with *oṃ vajrarakṣa haṃ*, one should wear an upper garment; and with *oṃ vajrauṣṇīṣa hūṃ phaṭ*, one should perform the uṣṇīṣa (topknot) rite.

Binding the eyes with the mantra *oṃ cakṣurbandhana-mocanāya hūṃ*, and having taken hold of the flower garland with *ākhaṃ vīra hūṃ* while offering it, [the substances] are consecrated with water using the mantra of all activities (*sarvakarmika*). Then, the yoginī or the one possessing the activity-vajra (*karmavajrin*) takes hold [of the disciple], and then she shall ask her own disciple: "Who are you, O lover of pleasure (*suratapriya*)?
(The reading *suratapriyaḥ* is noted as a variant).
Then the disciple should also say: "I am fortunate, O Great Bliss!"
Then one should question one's own disciple: "O you who delight in joy, who are you? Those disciples should reply: "I am the fortunate one, [dwelling] in great bliss."

Then, having caused him to generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) while reciting, "Oṃ, I generate the mind of all yoga," and having held the vajra with flowers to his heart while reciting, "Oṃ, you are the commitment of the Good Joy; Hoḥ! Accomplish, O Vajra, as is fitting," [the teacher says]: "Today you shall be empowered by all the Tathāgatas; and you must not speak of this supreme secret of all the Tathāgatas to anyone who has not entered the maṇḍala."

Having said, "And this must not be doubted," and having drawn [the disciple] in while reciting *oṃ āḥ yamāntakṛt hūṃ*, and having caused him to enter within the curtain with the mantra *āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ*, he should cause him to circumambulate while reciting, "O Great Joy, well-firm, well-pleased, well-blissful, O Vajrasattva, grant me success today! and to bow down at the eastern gate of the maṇḍala with palms joined and arms extended, uttering this mantra:
*pūrvadvārībāhuprasārya*.

Then, reciting *oṃ sarvayogacittam utpādayāmi*, he generates the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Holding a vajra together with a flower at his heart, he recites: *oṃ suratasamayas tvaṃ hoḥ siddhyavajra yathāsukhaṃ*.

One should say: "Now all the Tathāgatas will bestow their blessing upon you; you, moreover, must not speak of this most secret maṇḍala of all the Tathāgatas to those who have not entered the maṇḍala, nor should you show it to those who lack faith. Having said this, one should lead them away while reciting: *Oṃ yamāntakṛta hūṃ*.

Having placed [the substances] inside the vessel with the mantra *āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ*, one should circumambulate clockwise while reciting *mahāratnasudhī dhīḥ saṃtoṣaya sukhavajrasattva ājñāsiddhyai māṃ*. Then, with palms joined, one should go outside the eastern gate of the maṇḍala and prostrate, while reciting these mantras.

Oṃ, I offer myself for the service and worship of all Tathāgatas; O Vajrasattva of all Tathāgatas, empower me! Oṃ, I offer myself for the service and worship of all Tathāgatas; O Vajravairocana of all Tathāgatas, empower me! [To the south, with palms joined at the heart: Oṃ, I offer myself for the consecration of the worship of all Tathāgatas; O Vajraratna of all Tathāgatas, consecrate me! [To the west, with palms joined at the forehead:]

Oṃ, I offer myself for the performance of worship to all Tathāgatas. O Vajradharma of all Tathāgatas, cause me to turn [the wheel of Dharma]. With palms joined at the heart in the northern direction: Oṃ, I offer myself for the activity of worship to all Tathāgatas. O Vajrakarma of all Tathāgatas, act for me. Having thus bowed to the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, with these five mantras, one should again extend the arms at the eastern gate and say: Oṃ, I offer myself for attendance upon the feet of the Guru.

"Oṃ, for the sake of protecting all sentient beings, I offer myself. Thus one should cause [the practitioner] to recite this, preceded by a thorough understanding of its meaning. Having prostrated, he extends his arms toward the eastern door.

oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjopasthānāyātmānaṃ niryātayāmi sarvatathāgatavajrasattvādhiṣṭhasva māṃ | oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāupasthānāyātmānaṃ niryātayāmi sarvatathāgatavajraverocanādhiṣṭhasva māṃ | Joining the palms at the heart in the south.

oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjābhiṣekāyātmanāṃ niryātayāmi | sarvatathāgatavajraratnābhiṣiñca māṃ | [Joining the palms at the forehead in the west: oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāpravartanāyātmanāṃ niryātayāmi | sarvatathāgatavajradharmān pravartaya māṃ |

In the north, with palms joined at the heart, one causes [the practitioner] to prostrate to the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, through the five families, reciting: *oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjākarmaṇe ātmānaṃ niryātayāmi | sarvatathāgatavajrakarma kuru māṃ*. Then, once again from outside the eastern gate, with great devotion...
"oṃ guru tsaraṇopasthānāyātmanāṃ niryātayāmi | oṃ sarvasattvaparidraṇārthāyātmanāṃ niryātayāmi. One should have [the practitioner] recite these while preceded by an understanding of their meaning.

"Therefore, having today entered the family of all the Tathāgatas, I shall generate in you the vajra-knowledge by means of which you will attain even the accomplishments of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments. You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest your samaya be violated. Having said this, he places the vajra on [the disciple's] head while ringing the bell.
"This is your pledge (*samaya*): the vajra shall split your head if you speak of this to anyone. Having said this, he again places the vajra at [the disciple's] heart and says:
"Vajrasattva himself has today taken up residence within your heart."
If he should speak this policy, one should depart at that very moment, having broken through by oneself.

Having caused him to take an oath with the words "brūyād imaṃ" (he should say this), one should give [the water] from the mouth of the vessel held by the ring finger and thumb— containing the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), placed in a lotus bowl, consecrated with the three-syllable mantra, situated atop the victory flask (*vijayakalaśa*), and empowered by reciting "oṃ vajrāmṛtodaka ṭhaḥ" seven times— into his own mouth. This constitutes the oath.

"Then, since you have now entered the lineage of all the Tathāgatas, I shall therefore generate vajra-wisdom within you. By means of this wisdom, you will even attain the siddhi of all the Tathāgatas; what need is there to mention other siddhis?"

"You must not speak of this in the presence of those who have not seen the mandala; otherwise, your samaya will be impaired. Having said this, he should hold a vajra to the head and ring the bell, saying: "By this vajra of your samaya, if you speak of this to anyone, your head shall shatter!"

Again, holding the vajra at the heart, one makes this pledge with the words: "Today Vajrasattva truly dwells within your heart; if you speak of this method, he will immediately rend [your heart] and depart. Having thus made the pledge, the five nectars contained in a lotus vessel, consecrated with the three syllables, are placed atop the *vijaya* vase.
Recite "oṃ vajrāmṛta udaka ṭhaḥ" seven times. Holding the vessel with the ring finger and the thumb, pour it from the mouth of the vessel into his mouth:
"This is the water of hell for you; it shall burn upon the transgression of the samaya.
Through the preservation of the samaya, there is accomplishment. Drink this vajra-amṛta water!"
Having recited this and caused [the disciple] to drink from the vessel, he should say:

"From this day forward, I am Vajrapāṇi to you; whatever I tell you to do, that must be performed by you. You must not disregard me, lest through the failure to avoid poison you meet your end and fall into hell."
Thus is the offering of water according to the convention.

% Tib. gloss: the offering of the water of the pledge % "This is your hell-water; it shall burn you if you transgress the pledge. If you guard the pledge, it is the attainment of siddhi; therefore, drink this vajra-nectar water! Having spoken thus, he causes him to drink the water of *maṇi*. Then [he says]: "From this day forward, I am your Vajrapāṇi. Whatever I command you to do, saying 'Do this,' that you must perform."
"You must not treat me with contempt; otherwise, you will die without having abandoned your attachments and fall into hell"—thus one should speak. This is the bestowal of the water of the samaya.
Then, for the sake of his own immersion and for the attainment of all accomplishments, the disciple, being composed, should repeat the words prompted by the master.
"May all the Tathāgatas consecrate what has been spoken by the Ācārya, and may Vajrasattva enter into me."

Thereafter, the disciple says this: "May [the descent] be brought about through my own meditative equipoise; through the words of exhortation from the master, may all the Tathāgatas grant their blessing for the sake of perfectly accomplishing all siddhis. May Vajrasattva descend upon me!"
Then,
having meditated upon the body as being hollow from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
One should meditate upon a circle of fire accompanied by wind beneath his feet.
And above that, one should visualize the syllable *jhraiḥ*, red in color;
with the streams of light rays arising from it, the practitioner should purify his body.
Having thus rendered [the disciple] radiant, the practitioner,
for the sake of emerging from meditative absorption,
should again perform the placement of the syllables *hūṃ*, *haḥ*, and *āḥ* upon the heart, throat, and head of the disciple.
Having taken up the bell that effects possession, the practitioner should ring it with grandeur;
for the purpose of invoking the descent of the Tathāgata, he should recite this mantra.
"This is your commitment, the Vajra known as Vajrasattva;
it causes you this very day to enter into the unsurpassed Vajra-gnosis."
Oṃ vajrāveśa aḥ aḥ aḥ aḥ! If [the deity] does not enter even while reciting this mantra firmly in this manner:
Then, with the rays of the syllable *Aḥ*, one should impel the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*).
"Enter! Shake! Ra ra ra ra! Move! Move! Hūṃ haḥ āḥ jhaiḥ!
A trembling of the heart, horripilation, or even fainting and dancing, as well as falling back and forth—know these to be the signs of possession.
Having seen that the disciple is intent on the ritual seat (*viṣṭara*), the adept should place the syllable *ĀḤ* upon his tongue;
having stabilized it with the hundred-syllable mantra, he should ask about what is auspicious or inauspicious.
Then, the knower of mantras should gradually withdraw that possession by means of this sequence.

Having drawn in the descended deity with rays from one's own heart and caused her to enter within the seed-syllable of one's own heart, one should hold a vajra over the head of the disciple and dismiss [the deity] with "Oṃ kṛto vaḥ" and so forth, followed by "Hūṃ Haḥ Āḥ Jhaiḥ Mur. This is the procedure for the descent [of the deity].

Then, one should visualize all the apertures of the body from the soles of the feet upward; beneath those feet, one should meditate on a blazing mandala of fire. Above that, one should visualize a syllable *Dhīṃ* of red color. By the fiery radiance arising from it, the practitioner (*vratin*) purifies the bodies, and likewise illuminates the light.

Having performed the ritual of taking up [the empowerment], the wise one should then place *hūṃ*, *haḥ*, and *āḥ* upon the heart, throat, and head of the disciple. Holding the bell while sounding its resonance, he should cause [the deity] to descend. For the purpose of causing the Tathāgatas to descend, this mantra should be recited: "This is the Samayavajra; it is proclaimed as Vajrasattva."

May this unsurpassed vajra wisdom descend this very day! Oṃ vajrāveśaya āḥ āḥ āḥ āḥ. If it does not descend, recite this mantra firmly: Then, with light rays from the syllable ĀḤ, thoroughly impel the wisdom-being (jñānasattva): Āveśaya stambhaya rara racalaya calaya hūṃ haḥ āḥ jñaiṃ.

Whether it causes trembling or the hair to stand on end, or causes fainting or dancing, even if one leaps upward, it should be understood as having the characteristic of descent. For the disciple who has entered [the practice] with joy and gazing, the letter *āḥ* should be placed upon the tongue; having stabilized it with the hundred-syllable mantra, the wise one should inquire about what is virtuous and non-virtuous. This is the method for causing the descent to be released.

One should know this through the sequence of mantras: having summoned the deities who have definitely entered [the mandala] by means of the light rays from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart, one dissolves them into the seed-syllable at the heart. Then, holding a vajra at the head of the disciple, one should request them to depart with the words *oṃ khyod kyis sems can don kun mdzad* (Oṃ, you who have accomplished all the aims of sentient beings) and so forth, preceded by *hūṃ haḥ āḥ jñeṃ muṃ*.
This is the ritual for the descent [of the deity].

Then, having asked the disciple facing the mandala, "What kind of appearance do you perceive with your eyes?", and having understood his suitability for the rites of pacification, enrichment, subjugation, or wrathful activity according to the sequence of the appearances he describes—whether white, yellow, red, dark, or black—the master should take hold of one [finger] of the two thumbs with his right hand holding a vajra. While performing the vajra-step gesture and reciting the *kuṇḍalī* mantra, he should cause him to circumambulate three times to the right and perform the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).

Then, having asked the disciple who is facing the mandala, "What appears to you when you look with your eyes? if he replies, "It appears white, yellow, red, green, and black," then [the teacher should perform] pacifying, enriching, magnetizing, and... [as appropriate] according to the sequence.

One should make [the disciple] understand that they are endowed with the fortune for the siddhi of wrathful activity (*abhicāra*). Grasping their two thumbs with the right hand together with a vajra, one should have them perform three circumambulations in the manner of a dance with the vajra-step while reciting the circling mantra, and then perform this consecration of truth:
"In this mandala, this disciple has been properly introduced by me."
May the lineage of these gods be as meritorious as that.
Whatever kind of accomplishment may be attained by him, in whatever lineage he is a vessel,
and whatever power of merit resides in that vessel— may all that likewise belong to him in this maṇḍala.
Having thus performed the empowerment by truth.

"In this authentic mandala, I shall initiate this disciple. May the deities, according to their respective families, likewise accord him his share of merit. What kind of siddhi will he attain? To which family is he a suitable vessel? And what is the power of his merit? May it become exactly like that within the mandala! Thus one should recite.

Then, having first taken a single fresh and light flower from the garland previously held—which has been consecrated with the syllable *trāṃ*—he should place it in the student's cupped hands. At that time, the student, having resolved that he himself is the Lord of the Mandala together with the members of the assembly, as if standing before him, resplendent with the three syllables, free from defilement, and empowered by the Guru; and having mentally entered that mandala while relying upon [the deity], should cast the flower upon his head.

"Oṃ, remain! O Vajra, be firm for me; be eternal for me; preside over my heart; grant me all accomplishments! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ! Accept this handful of flowers, O Lord! Hoḥ! Reciting this mantra, one should assign the practitioner's *kula* according to where the flower falls within the five lines, and should likewise bestow the corresponding yoga and observe the signs of accomplishment.

Then, from the previously held flower garland—which has been consecrated with the syllable *traṃ*—one should extract a fresh, non-withered flower and place it in the hands of the disciple as they join their palms. At that time, the disciple should have intense devotion toward the flower garland, while one should oneself visualize being luminous through the three syllables and free from sin.

Once the master has thus bestowed the blessing, the disciple, preceded by devotion, should mentally enter that maṇḍala—visualizing the Lord of the Maṇḍala together with the maṇḍala deities as being present before them—and cast a flower upon his head. Oṃ tiṣṭha vajradhīme bhava | śāśvato me bhava | hrīdayaṃ me |

By reciting the mantra: *ā ā dhī tiṣṭha sarva siddhi me prayaccha hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ pratiṣṭha kusumāñjalina atha hoḥ*, flowers fall within the five receptacles; in accordance with this, one should reveal their respective families and so forth, and also bestow their yogas. Thus, the siddhis are indicated.

If a flower falls upon the head, the *uṣṇīṣa*, or the *ūrṇā* of the Buddhas, then there is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā; if it falls on the eyes or the mouth, then there is the accomplishment of Mantra.

If it falls on the upper part [of the body], it is the highest; on the middle part, the middling; but on the lower part, it is the lowest. If it falls at a great distance from the *bimba*, success comes after a long time; if near, success is swift. Regarding the deities, however, one's own station—such as the *koṣṭha* and so forth—should be known by its division. If the flower falls between two deities, then that belongs to whichever deity the flower is closer to. If it is equidistant, there is success according to both rites. In that case, whichever family he has a preference for, that becomes his.

If [the flower] falls outside the five lines, one should throw it again up to three times. In that case, if it falls outside, there is only a minor accomplishment (*kṣudrasiddhi*). If it falls outside the outer circular lines or outside the outer vajra-garland, there is no accomplishment. One must not show the mandala to such a person; rather, having rendered them worthy through mantra-recitation and other means, they should be admitted on another occasion.

If the flower falls upon the Buddha’s head, the *uṣṇīṣa*, or the *ūrṇā-kośa*, then at that time there is the attainment of Mahāmudrā. If it falls upon the eyes or the face, then at that time there is the attainment of Mantra. [Falling] upon the upper part of the body is supreme; upon the middle part is middling; and upon the lower part is inferior. If it lands very far from the body, it will take a long time.

For those who are near, it is swiftly accomplished. The respective abodes of the gods are to be understood as being demarcated by squares and so forth; if one falls between two gods, then at that time, one will belong to the class of whichever flower one is closer to. In the case of equanimity, the result of both is accomplished; at that time, one will belong to the class of whichever [flower] one has faith in.

If it falls outside the outer boundary line (*re kha*), it should be discarded again up to three times; if it still falls outside there, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) will be minor. If it falls outside the outer circular lines or outside the vajra-garland (*vajrāvalī*), there is no accomplishment, and in such a case, the mandala should not even be shown.
Having established their fitness through the recitation of mantras and so forth, they should be introduced at another occasion.
Then, taking that flower and reciting "Oṃ, accept this, O being of great strength," he should bind it upon the head of the disciple.
[The phrase] "having taken" refers to the procedure for the garland consecration (*mālābhiṣeka*).

% Tibetan Gloss: The Garland Empowerment % Then, taking that flower and reciting *oṃ pratigṛhṇa tvaṃ imaṃ sattva mahābala*, it is tied upon the head of the disciple. This is the ritual for the manifest empowerment of the garland.

When this possession has occurred, after explaining the auspicious signs and so forth, one should stabilize the possession with the mantra "Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra," perform the inquiry regarding the appearance of the visual field and so on up to the binding of the head, and then dismiss the descended deity. However, they say that if there is an inability to perform the rite of possession, one should instead perform the inquiry regarding the appearance of the visual field and so on immediately after offering the water of the pledge (samayodaka).

Since there is no capacity [for the deity to remain] during the rite of entry (*āveśa*), once the deity has arrived here, at the conclusion of the recitation of "virtue" (*dge ba*) and so forth, one should stabilize the arrival with the mantra *oṃ tiṣṭha vajra*. Then, from the inquiry regarding the visual appearances (*cakṣurdarśana*) and so on, up until the binding of the head, the definitively entered deity should be requested to depart.

It is explained that for those who are incapable, one should perform the procedure of "lowering" [the deity], and immediately after bestowing the water of commitment (samayodaka), one should ask about the appearance of the eyes and so forth.
Thereafter, having visualized two blazing *oṃ*s in the two eyes of the disciple:
"The Vajrasattva himself, intent upon opening your eyes today, [is] consciousness (*saṃjñāna*)."
The all-seeing Vajra-eye opens up the unsurpassed [vision].

Reciting "Oṃ jñānacakṣuḥ hūṃ aḥ svāhā," one should remove the blindfold. Immediately thereafter, one should visualize two blazing Oṃ syllables upon the two eyes of the disciple. Then, while reciting "Today Vajrasattva himself strives to open your eyes; may he open all eyes with the unsurpassed vajra-eye. Oṃ jñānacakṣuḥ hūṃ aḥ," the covering should be removed.
Then, having said, "O Vajra, look! [the teacher says]:
"Look now at this mandala and generate faith."
You are born into the family of the Buddhas, empowered by mudrās and mantras.
Through the perfection of all accomplishments, you shall become the foremost of those bound by the samaya;
perform the worship of the mantras with the graceful union of the vajra and the supreme lotus.

Having recited this, he says, "Now, look at Hevajra! and then speaks as follows: "Now, by the force of your faith, look upon this very mandala; you are born into the family of the Buddhas, and you shall accomplish the secret mantras."
Then one should reveal the reality of the mandala in its proper sequence,
and one should also instruct upon the essential nature of all the deities.
For all [mandalas],
there should be a noble square of truth with the Brahma-abodes as its corners.
The gateway known as the means of integration is fourfold in each case.
The mind consisting of the faculty of faith and so forth arises from five ramparts;
the four bases of psychic power are its four types of gate-towers.
In its center, however, is the wheel resembling eight mandalas;
this indeed is the eightfold liberation that accomplishes all attainments.
The Noble Eightfold Path is always the support for the great mass of all accomplishments;
thus it is known as the eight pillars.
The mandala within the circle, which is the symbolic representation of the meaning of the *dharmadhātu* and has eight pillars—
this is indeed the mind-mandala, the supreme city of great liberation.
The meditative absorptions are the archways here, and likewise the primordial nature is the banners;
at the gates of awakening, the wish-fulfilling trees are the fruits that have come to fruition.
One should manifest the five Buddhas by means of the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates;
and the four goddesses, Locanā and the others, as having the intrinsic nature of earth and the other elements.
Likewise, Rūpavajrā and the others have the nature of the five sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, one should visualize Kṣitigarbha and the others as having the nature of the eye and so forth,
and the lords of wrath such as Yamāri and others as having the form of the arms and so forth.
"One whose nature is compassion should reveal to the disciple, in due order, the Buddhas such as Akṣobhya and the others who reside within the body-cakra and in the outer cakra."

Then, one should clearly elucidate the reality (*tattva*) of the mandala in its proper sequence. Furthermore, the essential nature of all those deities should be demonstrated. Through the Noble Truths, it becomes four-sided; through the Brahma-abodes, the corners [are formed]; and the gates are said to be the means of gathering. One should correctly understand each of the four [gates] as being composed of the mind, such as faith, the faculties, and so forth.

It arises perfectly within five enclosures; the four bases of miraculous power are those four door-frames. In its center is a wheel, equal to the eight mandalas; by means of these eight liberations, all accomplishments (*siddhis*) are thoroughly established. The entire mass of great accomplishments always becomes like pillars.

These eight branches of the noble path are explained as the "eight pillars. By way of symbolizing the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*, there is a mandala within the wheel; this very mandala of the mind is the supreme city of great liberation. Here, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are the archways, and the banners are likewise their very nature; the enclosure wall is the fruit of enlightenment.

At the gates are wish-fulfilling trees; by way of the nature of the five aggregates, the five Buddhas are perfectly revealed. The four goddesses, Locanā and the others, are the very nature of the [four] elements, earth and so forth. By way of the nature of the five objects of desire, they are likewise Rūpavajrā and the others. Furthermore, by way of the nature of the eye and the other [sense faculties], they are Kṣitigarbha and the others.

"The hands and so forth are taught as the lords of the wrathful deities, such as Yamāntaka and the rest. The Buddhas residing in the body-mandala are, in order, the protectors Akṣobhya and the others. To the disciples in the outer mandala, those whose nature is compassion should be made manifest."

"I have entered the great maṇḍala of the Vajra-maṇḍala; I have been shown the great maṇḍala of the Yoga-maṇḍala; I have been initiated into the great maṇḍala of the Guhya-maṇḍala. Having made him recite this, one should cause him to hear the pledge (*samaya*): "Hoḥ! Hoḥ! Hoḥ! This is the procedure for the entry of the disciple.

% Tib. gloss: Initiating the Disciples % "I have entered the great mandala, the vajra mandala. I have seen the great mandala, the yoga mandala. I have been empowered in the great mandala, the secret mandala. Having had [the disciple] recite this, the samaya should be proclaimed: "Ho! Ho! Ho! This is the ritual for initiating the disciples.
Thereafter, having given a fee to the guru according to one's means for the purpose of the water-consecration, with knees placed upon the ground and palms joined in reverence:
"Just as the Great Festival was bestowed by Bodhivajra upon the Buddhas..."
For the sake of my protection as well, O Khavajra and others, grant it to me now!
Reciting thus, one should make the request.

Following that, for the purpose of the water empowerment, one should offer whatever wealth has been acquired to the guru, then place the knees upon the ground and join the palms, making this supplication while reciting: "Just as the Great Offering was bestowed Upon the Buddha Bodhivajra, So too, for the sake of my protection, O Vajra of Space, grant it to me today. Thus one should pray.
Then, outside the mandala, the mantra-practitioner should draw a square mandala with four openings in the eastern direction or in the northeast.
It should be two cubits in size and consist of two layers; in its center is a universal lotus (viśvapaṅkaja), and one should draw three enclosures in white, red, and black.
Having formed a perimeter with colored powder, one should place four mudrās:
the wheel in the east, the jewel in the south, the lotus with its filaments in the west, and the crossed-vajra in the north; having thus established them, one should set down the ritual vases.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the bathing mandala.
