Ritual of Ablution % Then, outside the mandala, in the eastern direction, the mantra practitioner should draw another mandala—either in the northeast—or one that is square with four doors, two cubits in size and having two tiers. In its center is a variegated lotus, and around it one should draw three enclosures of white, red, and black. Having prepared the colored powders for the enclosures, the four mudrās should be arranged there.

"In the east, a wheel; in the south, a jewel; in the west, a lotus together with its filaments; in the north, a treasure-giver and a crossed-vajra (viśvavajra) should be placed; a flask should also be set out. This is the ritual for the bathing maṇḍala.
Having brought that disciple who has performed the *kṛtamālā* consecration into the mandala,
one should establish him in the center of the lotus, making him assume the pride (*garva*) of the deity.
The Master, together with his retinue, should perform the consecration for the vajra-disciple,
reciting verses preceded by auspicious benedictions while using the jars that have been drawn up.
The Victors, holding vases filled like sesame pods,
now consecrate you; knowing this, be joyful in mind.
Having said, "O Sumanābhāva," one should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the disciple, who has been visualized in the form of Vajradhara, according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having performed the garland empowerment, the preceptor, maintaining the divine pride (*devatā-māna*), should take hold of the disciple and place them correctly upon a lotus in the center of the maṇḍala. Then, preceded by verses of auspicious benediction (*svastyayana*), the vajra-disciple should be bathed with the waters originating from the vases by the preceptor together with the assembly. [The vases] are filled like a heap of sesame seeds.

"O Victors who hold the vase, today we shall empower you; knowing this, let your minds be joyful. Having spoken thus, one should visualize the disciple in the form of Vajradhara and purify him according to the ritual previously described.

Thereafter, having summoned the Tathāgatas and the Vidyā-devis residing in the infinite directions by means of the rays of light from the seed-syllable in the heart, and having worshipped them for the sake of conferring initiation upon the disciples— {191b6} "The initiation of the Buddhas was indeed performed by the Vajrī for the protection of the world."
Just as Guṇākara was given [to us], so indeed should you give to him.
Just as the Vajra-holder bestowed empowerment upon the Buddha for the sake of protecting wandering beings, and granted him a source of qualities, so too, please bestow it upon this person.

Having thus made this supplication with the verse, those Tathāgatas, having entered into meditative absorption on wisdom, melted through great passion; entering within by way of the door of Vairocana, they emerged through the path of the vajra. With those fluids, the disciple—who had been introduced into the lotus of the Goddess by way of her mouth—was instantly consecrated following the state of emptiness as the form of Akṣobhya together with Prajñā, born from the syllable *HŪṂ* and non-different from the Jñānasattva. Then, emerging from their lotuses with bodies possessing arms, faces, and so forth, they remained filling the expanse of space.

Together with the vidyās such as Locanā and the others, [he visualizes] the disciples— having emerged from the lotus and being consecrated by the goddesses such as Rūpavajrā— with showers of parasols, banners, flags, garments, musical instruments, songs, dances, flowers, incense, saffron, and so forth, and with cool jars filled with the nectar of bodhicitta held in their sprout-like hands; having thus consecrated them instantaneously.
When he had thus offered this prayer in verse, those Tathāgatas, having entered into meditative equipoise through wisdom, were melted by great passion.

Having entered through the gateway of Vairocana and emerged via the vajra path, those seminal essences enter the lotus of the goddess from the mouth [of the disciple]. At that very instant, the disciple—following upon emptiness—is consecrated as the inseparable wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) in the form of Akṣobhya together with Prajñā, born from the syllable *hūṃ* and the vajra.

Furthermore, from the lotuses of the bodies of the hands, faces, and so forth, there emerged the Vidyās such as Locanā and others, filling the expanse of space; together with them, they offered parasols, victory banners, pennants, garments, the sounds of music, songs, dances, rains of flowers, incense, and saffron.

With their hands slightly tilted, they hold white vases, slightly tilted and filled with the *bodhicitta*; as they are being consecrated, these disciples are drawn forth from the lotuses by goddesses such as Rūpavajrā and the others, [chanting]:
"A further auspiciousness to the one who dwells in the hearts of all sentient beings, the universal self, the supreme lord of all families!"
May that auspiciousness of the great bliss which gives birth to all sentient beings without exception be yours today during the supreme consecration. (24)
May whatever auspiciousness dwells in the hearts of all sentient beings [abide here].
The self-nature of all, the supreme lord of all families.
The Great Bliss that gives birth to all sentient beings without exception.
May you be brought to peace through this supreme empowerment bestowed upon you today.
Whatever auspiciousness belongs to him who is endowed with the entire Vajra family, who purifies the people overcome by hatred,
and who bears the name Lord Akṣobhya—
May that auspiciousness be yours today at your supreme consecration.
May whatever auspiciousness exists in its entirety belong to the Vajra family.
The subduer of hatred, the purifier of all beings.
He who bears the name known as the Protector Akṣobhya.
May there be auspiciousness for you today as you receive this supreme empowerment!
Whatever auspiciousness belongs eternally to Vairocana— who is endowed with the entire family of delusion, who removes the suffering of existence,
and who purifies the people overcome by delusion— [may that auspiciousness be yours].
May that auspiciousness attend you today at your supreme consecration.
May whatever auspiciousness exists for all those belonging to the lineage of delusion—
Vairocana, who constantly robs [beings] of the suffering of existence.
Overpowering delusion, he is the one who fully enjoys all beings.
May there be auspiciousness for you today as you receive this supreme empowerment!
Whatever auspiciousness belongs to him who is endowed with the entire lineage of jewels,
who is intent upon liberating [beings] from the suffering of poverty,
and who purifies the people overcome by pride—
May that auspiciousness be yours today at your supreme consecration.
May whatever auspiciousness is endowed with every kind of jewel [bring about] well-being!
He exerts himself for the sake of being completely liberated from the suffering of poverty.
He who completely purifies all beings by subduing pride.
May there be auspiciousness for you today as you receive this supreme empowerment!
Furthermore, may there be *maṅgala* for Lokeśvara, who is endowed with the entire Padmakula and who rends the cage of worldly existence.
May that auspiciousness of the one who purifies people overcome by passion be yours today at this supreme consecration. 28.
May all auspiciousness belonging to the entire Lotus family be present!
Lord of the World, you who destroy the nets of worldly existence,
The person who completely enjoys [the world] while overcoming desire,
May there be auspiciousness for you today as you receive this supreme empowerment!
Whatever auspiciousness belongs to him who is endowed with the lineage of all virtuous deeds,
who is compassionate toward those addicted to false speech,
and who dispels that [falsehood] through mines of means for purification— may that [auspiciousness] [be yours].
May that auspiciousness be yours today at your supreme consecration.
May whatever auspiciousness exists, endowed with all the classes of karma, [be present].
To those who delight in speaking falsehoods, he is the very embodiment of compassion.
These are the antidotes that liberate one from the sin of envy;
by means of them, may there be auspiciousness for you today at this supreme empowerment!
Lakṣmīdhara, resembling a mountain of gold, lord of the three worlds, free from the three impurities—
the Buddha, whose eyes are like the petals of a fully blossomed lotus.
May that auspiciousness bring you peace today. || 30 ||
Possessing perfect excellence, like a mountain of gold;
Protector of the three worlds, who has abandoned the three stains.
The Buddha, who possesses eyes like the fully blossomed petals of a lotus;
May there be auspiciousness for you, who have long been peaceful!
You are the preeminent one taught by Tena, unshakable,
renowned throughout the three worlds, and honored by men and gods.
May that supreme Dharma, which brings peace to all living beings, be a source of auspiciousness and peace for you today. (31)
The supreme, most excellent, and immovable [state] taught by him—
Renowned throughout the three worlds and honored by gods and humans.
The sublime Dharma brings peace to all living beings.
May there be peace and auspiciousness for you for a long time!
May the Saṅgha, endowed with the True Dharma, rich in the auspiciousness of learning, and worthy of offerings from humans, gods, and asuras, [grant you well-being].
May that most excellent one among the hosts, the abode of modesty and glory, grant you auspiciousness and peace this day. 32.
The Saṅgha possesses the auspicious wealth of hearing the sublime Dharma;
it is the worthy recipient of offerings from humans, gods, and asuras.
The supreme excellence of the assembly, the foundation of modesty and glory.

"May there be auspiciousness for you, who are long-lived and bring peace," and so forth—with such auspicious songs being offered, he himself should sing them. First, with the water from the *vijaya*-vase, then from the vases of the four Tathāgatas, then from the vases of the four goddesses, and then from the vases of the maṇḍala deities as appropriate—water which is the nature of the nectar of *bodhicitta*, held in the left fist with its fingers covered by sprouts and the right hand holding a *vajra*, and poured from the tip of the *vajra*—[he should perform the consecration].

While auspicious songs such as these are being performed to bring about good fortune, one should also join in those songs; first, the vase of complete victory (*vijaya-kalaśa*), then the vases of the four Tathāgatas, and thereafter the vases of the four goddesses.

Then, as appropriate, one should pour from the tip of the vajra held in the right hand in a fist-like grip—along with its prongs—the water from the maṇḍala vases, which is of the nature of the nectar of bodhicitta, while reciting:
"Oṃ, I consecrate you with the empowerment of Mahāsukha Vajrasattva, so that you may become firm in your sovereignty over all Tathāgatas."
Reciting: *oṃ mahāsukhavajrasattva ābhīṣekena tvām abhiṣiñcāmi sarvatathāgatādhipati treyadhvavyāpī bhava*, [one says]:
"I bestow the great vajra empowerment, which is venerated by the three realms, arising from the source of the three secrets of all Buddhas. (33)
The great empowerment vajra, honored by those of the three realms.
The three secrets of the Vajra have truly arisen; they shall be bestowed by all the Buddhas.
Reciting "Oṃ āḥ, consecrate with the vajra-water, hūṃ! You are I in supreme bliss," one should perform the consecration.
One should perform the manifest empowerment by reciting: *oṃ āḥ vajra udaka abhiṣiñca hūṃ surate āḥ haṃ*.

Alternatively, in the absence of a bathing mandala, one should seat the disciple at the eastern gate of the mandala, draw small amounts of water from the victory-pitchers and other vessels, hold it in a lotus-bowl or a conch shell, and sprinkle him according to the prescribed sequence.

Furthermore, if there is no bathing mandala, one should place the disciples at the eastern gate of the mandala, collect a small amount of water from the *vijaya* and other vases, pour it into lotus bowls or conch shells, and confer the empowerment.

And in the event that a powder mandala is not possible, one should perform the consecration as before using only the water from the Victorious Vase—which is of the nature of Akṣobhya and consists of the nectar of bodhicitta—upon a mandala drawn on cloth or similar material.

Even if a mandala of colored powders is not available, one should perform the empowerment through the very water of the *vijaya*-vase— which is the nature of Akṣobhya— by way of the essence of bodhicitta, within a mandala situated on cloth or similar materials.

One should contemplate: "At that time, they become absorbed in great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Thus, the water initiation is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). In some places, it is called the perfectly pure wisdom of the sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*).
This refers to the water empowerment, which is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). According to some, it is the wisdom of the utterly pure sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*).
Having received the water-consecration and emerged from the bathing circle,
one should take up the ornaments from the side of the great maṇḍala.
Through the stages of the bathing mandala, one correctly receives the water empowerment; as for those who properly take up the ornaments, it is on the surface of the great mandala.
Having become one wearing variegated garments or even red garments, adorned with royal ornaments...
holding a white parasol, he is gladdened by this music. || 35 ||
Clad in red garments and adorned with the ornaments of the Victorious One.
Properly donning the white crown, one should bring joy with this song.
O Great Bliss, Great Passion, Great Vajra, Great Wealth, O Great Wisdom, O Great Knowledge! O Vajrasattva and the rest, grant me accomplishment! 36.
Great bliss, great passion, the great vajra, the great treasure.
O Great Wisdom, O Great Gnosis, may I today accomplish the state of Vajrasattva.
O Great Vajra of all Buddhas, bestower of all accomplishments and bliss; O you who grant all empowerments and all aims, the unsurpassed sovereignty of the vajras! (37)
The great vajra of all buddhas, the unsurpassed lord of vajras.
For the sake of all [beings], bestow the supreme bliss of all accomplishments through every empowerment.
Victory to you, O giver of the ultimate reality of the primordial Buddha!
Victory to you, O giver of the wealth of Dhamma that grants both desire and liberation! Victory to you, O great one who possesses the five supernormal knowledges! Victory! Victory!
Go, O Vajrapāṇi, great bliss! Ha! Ha!
Oops, this should be revised...
As it truly is, the Primordial Buddha is the bestower of ultimate bliss.
One who bestows liberation, wealth, and the Dharma exactly as desired.
It acts as a companion to the five primordial wisdoms and to supreme joy.
Just as Vajrapāṇi himself is the protector of great bliss, so too [is he].
DZA Ā ĀI BUDDHĀ SARAMA THE DE HA AO.

DZA Ā VAJRA BĀṆI MAHĀ SUHAṆA AO.
Thereafter, the Guru should perform three circumambulations of the mandala from the right.
Then, having seated him on a soft, wide cushion at the eastern gate, the Guru shall empower the disciple with the consecration of all the Buddhas. (38)
Once again, here one should perform three circumambulations of the Guru’s mandala.
Then, having opened the door, one who dwells in the east shall enter.
Through the empowerment of all the Buddhas, the Guru shall gather the disciples.
Having placed the mudrās upon the middle of the head, the forehead, the two sides of the head, and the back, one should recite these mantras. || 39 ||
One should correctly place the mudrā upon the center of the head, the two sides, likewise the crown, and also upon the back; then this mantra should be recited.
Oṃ vajradhātvīśvari abhiṣiñca hūṃ | Oṃ sattvavajri abhiṣiñca bhrūṃ | Oṃ ratnavajri abhiṣiñca trāṃ |

Oṃ dharmavajri abhiṣiñca hrīḥ | Oṃ karmavajri abhiṣiñca aḥ | Oṃ vajradhātviśvari abhiṣiñca hūṃ | Oṃ sattvavajri abhiṣiñca bhrūṃ | Oṃ ratnavajri abhiṣiñca hrāṃ | Oṃ dharmavajri abhiṣiñca hrīḥ | Oṃ karmavajri abhiṣiñca trāṃ |
Having recited the verse beginning with "The great vajra empowerment" (*abhiṣekaṃ mahāvajram*) and so forth,
as well as the mantra: *oṃ āḥ vajramakuṭābhiṣiñca hūṃ suratas tvam aham*.
Reciting "oṃ āḥ vajramukuṭābhiṣiñca hūṃ | suratastvam ahaṃ," and again with the mantra "oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ," one binds the crown on the forehead;
then once more, with the mantra "oṃ hūṃ hrāṃ hrīḥ āḥ," one ties the silk streamers at the brow.
Reciting "Vajra tuṣya hoḥ," one should please [the deity] through equanimity. This is the crown initiation, the gnosis of equanimity.
This refers to the empowerment of the crown, which is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
Then, having transformed the syllable *hrīḥ* and the lotus into the form of Amitābha, inseparable from the Jñānasattva, and holding the vajra—
which is of the nature of Amitābha— at the heart of the disciple:
"Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration."
Take this, which is the state of all Buddhas, as the vajra for the sake of perfect accomplishment. || 40 ||
Today, I shall bestow upon you the vajra empowerment of the Buddhas.
Hold this vajra for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of all the Buddhas.
Reciting thus, having touched the disciple’s heart, throat, and head with the vajra, he should place the vajra in the disciple’s right hand.
Having spoken thus, one should touch the heart, throat, and head of the disciple with the vajra and bestow the vajra in the right hand.
This is the vajra empowerment, the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
This refers to the vajra empowerment, which is the wisdom of individual discernment.

Then, having placed in the disciple’s left hand the bell—which has been transformed into Amoghasiddhi—and [the disciple] having become the form of Khavajra-Amoghasiddhi, non-different from the Jñānasattva, and having caused him to perform the gesture of embracing the mudrā with both hands joined by the vajra and the vajra-bell;

Then, the disciple—who is inseparable from the wisdom-being (jñānasattva) in the form of Amoghasiddhi, born from the *khaṭvāṅga* and sword—is given a bell that has been completely transformed into Amoghasiddhi. Having been made to perform the manner of embracing the mudrā with hands holding a vajra and a bell, [the preceptor] recites:
"Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Lord of Vajras; abide, O Vajra; you are the Samaya."
Reciting: *oṃ vajrādhipate tvaṃ abhiṣiñcāmi tiṣṭha vajrasamayas tvaṃ*, and saying:

*oṃ vajraghaṇṭā āḥ āḥ | gṛhīto 'si mayā bhagavan mayi saṃnihito bhava*, one should cause [the disciple] to recite: *oṃ vajraghaṇṭe āḥ āḥ | bcom ldan 'das gzung ngo bdag la ni || yang dag nye bar gyur par mdzod*.
Thus is the bell-consecration, which is the knowledge for the performance of activities.
Thus it is said: this is the empowerment of the bell, which is the wisdom of accomplished activity.
Thereafter, having visualized oneself as the form of Vairocana born from the syllable OṂ, of one flavor with the Jñānasattva, one should firmly hold the vajra and vajra-bell at the head.

Following that, one should contemplate the form of Vairocana, arising from the syllable *oṃ* and the wheel, as being of one taste with the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*). Then, holding the vajra and bell evenly at the head, recite: *oṃ vajrasattva tvām abhiṣiñcāmi vajranāmābhiṣekataḥ | he śrī-amuka-vajranāma-tathāgata siddhya samayas tvaṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*.
oṃ vajrasattva tvām abhiṣiñcāmi vajranāmābhiṣekataḥ | O Glorious One named [Name], Tathāgata Vajra, may there be accomplishment for you; samayas tvaṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ!
Thus, with the name of one’s own family lineage following the falling of the flower, one should consecrate [the disciple] as the essence of Vairocana.
Thus, following the falling of the flower, one should be consecrated by the nature of Vairocana, whose name corresponds to one's own family.

In this regard, the names of Vajrasattva are: Paramādya, Anutpanna, Surata, Samarasa, Vijaya, Alala, Sattva, Mahāsukha, Anaṅga, Jñāna, and Sahajavajra. The word "vajra" should be connected to each [of these]. The same applies to the names of the six Tathāgatas as well.

The names of Vajrasattva are: Supreme Primordial, Incomparable, Utterly Joyful, Equal Taste, Victorious, Āla-la, Hero, Great Bliss, Limbless, Gnosis, and Coemergent Vajra. To each of these, the term "Vajra" should be prefixed.
These are indeed the names of the six Tathāgatas.
Of Akṣobhya: Hāsa, Vilāsa, Rati, Līlā, Lalita, Svayambhū, Dveṣa, He, Karuṇā, Cintā, and Hūṃkāra are the Akṣobhyavajras.
The names of the Vajras are: Akṣobhya’s laughter, the graceful, joy, elegance, playfulness, self-arisen, hatred, ha, compassion, mind, the performer of HŪṂ, and Vajra.
Of Vairocana: Oṃkāra, eternal Tathāgata, delusion-illusion, Buddha-form body, Vairocanavajra!
[These are] Vairocana, Oṃkāra, Nitya, Tathāgata, Moha, Māyā, Buddha, Rūpa, Kāya, Vairocana, and Vajra.
Of Ratnasambhava: the wish-fulfilling jewel, space, splendor, the sun, the maker of light, pride, and the vajra of jewels.
[The deities] of Ratnasambhava are: Cintāmaṇi, Kha, Ākāśa, Tejas, Mārajit, Prabhāsa, Māna, and Ratnavajra.
Of Amitābha: Rāgāvalokita, Dharmapadma, Vajrāṅkura, Padmāṅkura, Suratāṅkura, Amitasuratānanda, Paramānanda, Karuṇāṅkura-vāk, and Amitābhavajra.
[They are] the passion of Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, Dharma, Padma, Vajrāṅkura, Pramodaṅkura, Amita, Padmāṅkura, Paramānanda, Pramodānanda, Karuṇāṅkura, Vāc, and Amitābhavajra.
Of Amoghasiddhi: Paramāśva, Samaya, Pāramitā, Karma, Anila, Anilaya, Sparśa, Īrṣyā, and Amoghavajrā.
Anilaya, Amoghasiddhi-vajra, the supreme horse, the samaya, the supreme, the perfection, the activity, wind, tangibility, envy, and Amogha-vajra.
The family women of Vajrasattva are Vajravegā, Vajravilāsinī, Vajramadā, Vajrakoṅkaṇā, Vajrānanā, Vajrapatākā, Vajramālā, and Vajrodayā.
Among women, there are Vajrasattva’s Vajravegā, Vajralāsyā, Vajramadā, Vajrakoṅkānā, Vajramukhī, Vajramālā, and Vajrodgatā.
Of Akṣobhya: Vajranairātmyā, Vajrahastā, Vajrāvalī, Vajrakarā, Vajramāmakī, and Dveṣarati.
These are Akṣobhyavajrā, Nairātmyā, Vajrahastā, Vajramālā, Vajramāmakī, and Dveṣarati.
Of Vairocana: Vajraḍākinī, Vajragaurī, Buddhaḍākinī, Vajravairocanī, Vajralāsyā, Vajralocanā, and Moharati.
Vairocanavajraḍākinī, Vajragaurī, Buddhakhecarī, Vajravairocanī, Vajralāsyā, Vajralocanā, and Moharatī.
Of Ratnasaṃbhava: Vajratārā, Vajrahārā, Vajraśvāsā, Vajrajvālā, Vajramānā, Mānavajrā, Vajrākāśā, Ākāśavajrā, and Ākāśarati.
Ratnasambhava’s Vajratārā, Vajradaṃṣṭrī, Vajrasānti, Vajrajvālā, Vajragarvā, Garvavajrā, Vajrākāśā, Ākāśavajrā, and Ākāśaratī.
Of Amitābha: Vajrarāgā, Rāgavajrā, Vajragītā, Vajrāhoḥsukhā, Vajravetālī, Vajramatī, Vajrahāsyā, Vajrapāṇḍarā, and Rāgarati.

[Vajramatī] (also in Tib.!): Vajraratī [Vajra-pleasure], Rāgavajrī [Vajra-passion], Vajragītā [Vajra-song], Vajrāṃbā [Vajra-mother-bliss], Vajravetālī [Vajra-vampire], Vajrabuddhi [Vajra-intellect], Vajrahāsā [Vajra-laughter], Vajrapāṇḍarā [Vajra-white-clad], and Rāgarati [Passion-delight].
Of Amoghasiddhi: Vajragarvā, Vajramāyā, Vajravaḍavā, Vajrahāsā, Vajranarteśvarī, Samayavajrā, and Vajrarati.
Amoghasiddhivajrā, Vajramāyā, Vajrahāsā, Vajranṛtyeśvarī, Samayavajrā, and Vajrarati.
The name-consecration is the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena. || o ||
This is the empowerment of names; it is the wisdom of the dharmadhātu, which is utterly pure.

In each of these aforementioned consecrations, one should perform the request with the verse beginning "By the Bodhivajra of the Buddhas... and the bathing with the verse beginning "The Great Vajra Consecration... and so forth.

For each of these aforementioned empowerments (*abhiṣeka*), one should make supplication with the verse beginning, "To the Buddha Bodhivajra... and so forth, and one should also perform the ritual ablution with the verse beginning, "The great vajra empowerment...

{194b3}. These six empowerments, starting with the garland and water empowerments, are called "knowledge empowerments" (*vidyā-abhiṣeka*) because they produce the fitness that is the antidote to ignorance.

These six empowerments, such as those of the rosary and water, are called the "empowerment of knowledge" (*vidyā-abhiṣeka*), which establishes the very capacity that serves as the antidote to ignorance.

A disciple consecrated by these empowerments becomes authorized for the hearing, exposition, and mantra-practice of the *Kriyā* and *Caryā* Tantras; however, he is not [authorized] for the *Yoga* and *Yoginī* Tantras—such is the opinion of those who consider themselves Ācāryas, which is a view lacking scriptural authority (*anāgama*). For nowhere did the Blessed One teach, nor was it logical, that the nature of those [higher tantras] could be described without the vow (*saṃvara*) of the innate empowerment (*sahajaseka*).
[The reading "ācāryamanyamatam" is supported by the edition; "anne ācāryamanyaṃmatam" is noted, but "na" is not.]

Regarding the sequence for conferring these empowerments: one is empowered to hear, explain, and practice the mantras of the Kriyā and Caryā Tantras. Furthermore, the claim that one desires the status of an *ācārya* [teacher] based on the statement, "Also the Yoga and Yoginī Tantras," is not supported by scripture.
For those who are devoid of innate power and vows, the Blessed One has not taught its own nature in any tantra, nor is it logical [to do so].

And these consecrations are bestowed upon those who do not seek the master’s consecration after first granting the common vows; however, for those who do seek it, they are bestowed preceded by the granting of both sets of vows.
Preceded by the bestowing of the vows (*saṃvaradānapūrvakaṃ*) / Preceded by the bestowing of the vows (*saṃvaradānapuraḥsaram*).
NB: End of Moriguchi II-1 (1992).

For those who do not seek these empowerments for the purpose of becoming an ācārya, they should be conferred preceded by the granting of the common vows. For those who do seek them, they should be conferred preceded by the granting of both sets of vows.
Then, [to the disciple] who has offered the fee and joined his palms in reverence,
[the master says]: "O treasure of compassion, grant me the Vajrācārya initiation!"
May I be capable of accomplishing the welfare of both myself and others through your grace.
Having recited this, one should visualize the disciple—who has performed the supplication to the guru—as HŪṂJA in the form of Vajrasattva.

Then, the disciple, having offered a gift and joined her palms, should address the guru with this prayer: "I pray that you, O treasury of compassion, grant me the empowerment of the Vajra Master, by whose grace I shall become capable of accomplishing the welfare of both myself and others. While she is thus supplicating, the guru should visualize himself in the form of Vajrasattva, born from the syllable *hūṃ*:
*anādinidhanaḥ sattvo vajrasattvo mahārataḥ* (The being without beginning or end, Vajrasattva, the Great Joy).
*Anne mahārataḥ*.
Samantabhadra is the self of all, the lord of Vajragarvā, the Lord.
Reciting "The Blessed One is the primordial supreme person," one should place the vajra in the right hand; this is the Vajra-samaya.

The bodhisattva who is without beginning or end is Vajrasattva, the Great Joy; he is Samantabhadra, the self-nature of all, the master of the lord Vajrasattva. Addressing him as "Bhagavān, the Supreme Primordial Being," one should place the vajra in his right hand; this is the Vajra-samaya.
Then, having meditated on the bell as being born from the syllable ĀḤ, [one should recite]:
"This is the bell of all the Buddhas, known to follow the resonance of sound;
it too must always be held by you, for supreme awakening is what the Victors have intended."
Having recited this, one should place the bell in the left hand; this is the commitment (*samaya*) of the bell.

Then, having visualized the bell as arising from the syllable ĀḤ, one should say: "This is explained as the resonance of the wisdom of all Buddhas; you too must always hold it, for the Victors desire supreme enlightenment. While reciting this, the bell should be placed in the left hand. This is the commitment (samaya) of the bell.
The disciple, however, [should ring] that bell:
"For existence is made non-existent by the natures of existence;
supreme existence is brought about by beings who are pure by nature."
Saying this, one should cause it to be played.

The disciple should also ring that bell while reciting: "Existence is pure by its very nature; it has been rendered free from existence by its very nature. It shall act as the sublime existence of the supreme, naturally pure Bodhisattva. Thus one should speak and ring it.
Following that:
"Indeed, the mudrā is declared to be the *samaya* because of the firmness of the mental form;
since it makes every form firm, it is therefore celebrated as 'mudrā'."
Having thus empowered the internal *jñānamudrā* by means of this [verse], one should perform the gesture of embracing; this is the *mudrā-samaya*. || O ||

Then, furthermore, the commitment of the mudrā (mudrā-samaya) was taught: "The body of the mind is itself stable; this is proclaimed as the commitment of the mudrā. Because it stabilizes this entire body, it is celebrated as the 'mudrā. By means of this, one should perform the manner of embracing with the hands that which is blessed as the wisdom-mudrā of the supreme self. This is the commitment of the mudrā.
As it is said in the *Paramādya*:
"Having grasped the vajra with the reality (*tattva*), and having sounded the bell with the Dharma,
one should empower the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) with the commitment (*samaya*) and recite the mantra from the heart."
Thus ends the procedure for bestowing the three pledges.

"Whatever was taught in the *Paramādya*, one should grasp that very vajra; having sounded the bell with the Dharma, one should empower the great mudrā of the samaya and recite the heart mantra. This is the ritual for bestowing the three samayas.

Thereafter, having visualized the disciple— who has received the three samayas— in the form of Vajrasattva, and having contemplated him being consecrated by the goddesses and Tathāgatas emerging from the seed-syllable in his heart while remaining in the sky,
[the teacher recites]: "I bestow the Great Vajra Consecration, honored by the three realms,
which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas."

Reciting "Oṃ āḥ, to the glory of the pledge of the consecration of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ svāhā," one should perform the consecration. Then, having visualized [the disciple] with Akṣobhya as his crown, one should cause other Tathāgata goddesses to enter that very form of the wisdom-being (jñānasattva). Having empowered him with the mantra "Oṃ supratiṣṭhitavajre svāhā," one should offer flowers and so forth to him. As it is said: "Embracing a sixteen-year-old Wisdom Consort (prajñā) with both hands, through the union of the bell and vajra, this is considered the Master’s consecration."
Thus [it is said].

Then, as for the taking up of the three pledges: one should visualize the disciple in the form of Vajrasattva. One should imagine that the goddesses exhorted by the seed-syllable at the heart and the Tathāgatas residing in the sky are bestowing empowerment, [reciting]: "The great vajra empowerment, which is prostrated to by the three realms..."

"The source from which the three secrets truly arise, may all Buddhas bestow it! By reciting "Oṃ āḥ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekatasamayaśrīye hūṃ," one should confer the empowerment. Then, visualizing Akṣobhya as the crown ornament, the other Tathāgatas and goddesses are introduced in the form of wisdom beings (jñānasattva).

One should consecrate [the disciple] with the mantra: *oṃ supratiṣṭha vajre svāhā*, and offer flowers and so forth to them. As it is said: "Embracing with the hands a sixteen-year-old woman endowed with wisdom, through the union of the vajra and bell, this is held to be the master’s initiation."
Thereafter, he should briefly explain the reality of the mandala and the purification of the mandala.
For the aggregates themselves are the stainless maṇḍala, thick with all the goddesses of definitive determination;
and therein, awakening is the hero Heruka, whose body is the natural outflow of the essence of suchness.
Thus ends the ritual for the consecration of the master, also known as the consecration of the vārtika.

Following that, the reality of the maṇḍala (*maṇḍalatattva*) and its purification (*viśuddhi*) shall also be briefly explained: "The maṇḍala is the stainlessness of the aggregates; it is definitively established as the assembly of all goddesses. Heruka and the Hero are likewise the Tathāgatas; there too, they are realized from the continuum of body and corpse. This refers to the irreversible empowerment (*avaivartikābhiṣeka*).
This is the ritual for the master’s initiation under another name.

Then, having visualized himself in the form of Vajrasattva, having worshipped and praised [the deity] with flowers and so forth, and having playfully struck the disciple with a single flower, he should say: Then, having visualized himself in the form of Vajrasattva, having worshipped and praised [the deity] with flowers and so forth, and having playfully struck the disciple with a single flower, he should say these words.
From this moment forth, sport with the Perfect Buddhas and their sons through the application of Vajragarva, by means of the supreme bliss of the worship of passion. ĀḤ!
From this moment forth, for the sake of sporting with the Perfectly Enlightened Ones together with their consorts, perform the offering of supreme joy and bliss through the yoga of Vajragarvā. Āḥ!
Having struck with playful grace using the garland, worship all the Buddhas.
May there be no separation—by these [words], the garland is indeed their ornament. Oṃ.
With graceful charm, cast this garland; it shall bind all the Buddhas. It shall never be separated from them; this garland is an ornament. Oṃ.
Sing the song of all the true Dharma for all embodied beings;
thereby you shall easily experience that attainment of a happy rebirth. (The Song)
Sing the song of the sublime Dharma for all embodied beings; by that, you shall attain the supreme bliss of the siddhi of the Sugatas. Gi!
Having offered the rhythmic clapping and danced, you shall delight the Perfectly Awakened Ones and perform the drama of the deeds of those to be trained by the Perfectly Awakened Ones. Hoḥ!
With the dance of palms joined together, out of devotion for the Perfectly Awakened One, perform the transformation into the manner of a dancer through the Buddha’s activity of taming beings! Ho!
O you of excellent vows, by wafting incense, gladden the Perfect Buddhas!
O you of excellent vows, through the knowledge of the Sugatas' entry, you shall cause embodied beings to enter [into that state]. A.
By offering incense to the Perfectly Awakened Ones, you have well-perfumed the body with the vows and commitments; thus, you shall attain the Sugata’s body through the manner of primordial wisdom.
ĀḤ | Having scattered flowers before the Buddhas, you shall further accumulate the factors of enlightenment and attain the Sugata’s body, endowed with the major marks and minor signs. BHRŪṂ |
Cast flowers upon the Buddhas! By becoming the accumulation of the branches of enlightenment, may you attain the body of a Sugata, endowed with the major marks and minor signs. BHRŪṂ!
Having fully kindled the eye of the Dharma, like Vajradharma himself, illuminate with the light of primordial wisdom those sentient beings blinded by ignorance. PRAṂ!
Having well kindled the fire of the Dharma, like a vajra-dharma, illuminate with the light of primordial wisdom the dark jungles of ignorance of sentient beings.

Having offered fragrance (*gandha*) to the Victors, turn the wheel of the Buddha for those who bestow gifts. [Bestow] ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. *Gaḥ*.

By offering incense to the Victors, one circles the bodies of those possessing enlightenment with ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision of the knowledge of liberation.
Then, one should personally recite the heart-mantra and other mantras either one hundred and eight times or three times.
Saying, "O Blessed One, you have been given by me; be present here," he should give [the initiation] to the disciple.

Then, having recited the mantra of one's own heart-essence (*hṛdaya*) and so forth one hundred and eight times or three times, one should say, "Blessed One, please grant this dhāraṇī; may you bestow it upon this [disciple]," and thus give it to the disciple.
The disciple also [should say]:
"O Blessed One, you are accepted by me; remain present within me.
Having grasped [the image] with these words, he should recite [the mantra] three times.
The disciple also recites this three times: "Bhagavān, I have received it; please grant me your favor."
Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of the mantra.
This is the ritual for the entrustment of the mantra.
Thereafter,
the knower of reality, using a probe made of the same material, should recite the mantra while applying honey, clarified butter, and collyrium poured into a golden or silver vessel.
Oṃ Vajranetrī, remove the veil! Hrīḥ!
Child, the veil of ignorance has been removed from you by the Victors, just as the King of Physicians removes the cataract of the world with a probe.
Thus one should say. This is the procedure for the collyrium.

Following this, having taken honey and medicinal ointment from a vessel of gold or silver with a probe, one who knows the reality of the mantra should anoint those very [eyes] with the mantra: *oṃ vajranetra āpahara pāṭalaṃ hrīḥ*. Just as the King of Physicians, holding the probe, removed the cataracts of the world, so too, my son, may you remove the cataract of ignorance.
"The Victors have cleared away the cataracts"—thus it should be recited; this is the ritual for the medicinal ointment for the eyes.
Then, having taken up a mirror consecrated with the syllable ĀḤ,
he should show it to the vajra-disciple while reciting this verse:
All phenomena are like reflections: transparent, pure, and unclouded;
they are ungraspable and inexpressible, yet arise from causes and karma.
Like a mirror, O Vajrasattva, you are clear, pure, and unclouded;
for within your heart, my child, resides the Lord of all Buddhas himself.

Having thus understood that all phenomena are indeed devoid of intrinsic nature and without abode, perform incomparable benefit for sentient beings; you have been born upon the breast of the Protectors.
Thus he should speak. This is the procedure for the mirror-gazing rite.

Then, taking up a mirror and consecrating it with the syllable *āḥ*, one should show it to the face of the disciple and recite this verse: "Phenomena are like reflections: Clear, pure, and unclouded; Inapprehensible and inexpressible, Arisen perfectly from causes and karma. Vajrasattva is like a mirror."

"It is pure and free from turbidity; the self-nature of all Buddhas has entered into your heart, my son. Having understood that phenomena are thus without intrinsic nature and without abiding place, perform incomparable benefit for sentient beings; you shall be born as a son of the Protectors. This is the ritual for showing the mirror.

Then, having recited "Hoḥ," one should give the bow produced from the syllable *hoḥ*, saying, "Make all the Tathāgatas rejoice. At the time of shooting the arrows, while the disciple recites, "Oṃ, I make all the Tathāgatas rejoice," four arrows should be shot in the four directions with the intention of piercing obstacles—one upward and another downward. This is the procedure for shooting the arrows.

Then, while reciting "HŪṂ" from the syllable HŪṂ and saying "Sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇasvāhā," the bow is bestowed. At the time of bestowing the empowerment, the disciple—while aiming at the obstructors with the intention of piercing them—should shoot arrows.
One is shot upward and the other downward; this is the ritual for shooting the arrows. || ||

In all these empowerments, one should perform the consecration while reciting: *oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye hūṃ svāhā*. Thus, by means of the master’s empowerment, there is the purification of the body.

One should confer empowerment by reciting "Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekatasamayaśrīye hūṃ svāhā" in all these empowerments; thus is the master's empowerment, which is the thorough purification of the body.

Then, having performed the commitment (*samaya*) according to the procedure of the Samayacakra to be described below, in a place made secluded by means of a curtain or similar screen, the disciple— having offered to the Guru for the sake of the secret initiation a consort (*prajñā*) adorned with beauty and youth, who is capable of maintaining the commitments and vows, or in her absence another— should there conceive of the Guru in the form of Vajrasattva and, with palms joined in reverence, say: "By the grace of your feet, I have attained the unsurpassed practice."
Therefore, O Lord, grant your grace by means of the secret initiation.
Thus one should entreat three times.

Then, having performed the commitment (*samaya*) of the assembly of the wheel (*cakrasamāja*) that will be explained hereafter, and having made [the area] secluded by means of a curtain and so forth, he adorns himself with physical beauty, youth, and the like, for the purpose of thoroughly instructing the disciple.

If a consort who possesses the commitments, meditative realization, and good fortune cannot be found, one may offer another suitable wisdom-consort to the guru for the sake of the secret meaning. Thereupon, with intense devotion toward the guru as Vajrasattva, one joins the palms and says: "Through the grace of your feet, I have attained the unsurpassed task; therefore, [grant] the secret empowerment."
"O Protector, please grant me your protection! Thus one should make this supplication three times.

Then, having emerged at the proper time, he sits upon the bow. Thereupon, the Guru, skilled in the three samādhis, performs the meditative union with her—who, following the realization of emptiness, has manifested in the form of a goddess from her former form as an ordinary woman—preceded by the honoring of the vajra and lotus.

Reciting "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra of the passion of all Tathāgatas," one visualizes that the Tathāgatas—Vairocana and the others—who have been summoned by the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart and have entered into union with Locanā and the other goddesses, enter oneself through the gate of Vairocana. Having become liquefied through great passion, one contemplates them emerging via the *avadhūtī* channel. Having stabilized the innate bliss within the vajra-jewel, one presses it with the thumb and ring finger, extracts the [vajra-jewel] from the lotus, and resolves that this liquid of the Tathāgatas is non-different from one's own bodhicitta.

Because of the fear that the disciple—who is of the nature of the Vajra of Speech—might lack faith upon seeing [the mandala], the blindfold of wisdom and means should be bound; having been held by a Yoginī or a Karmavajrī, he should be led inside. Having entered, he should prostrate with his knees touching the ground and offer a handful of flowers.

Then, having gradually established [the disciple] in the commitments (*samaya*), the virtuous master, through the three samādhis, should first generate the ordinary female form as the form of a goddess following upon emptiness; then, preceded by the ritual union of the vajra and the lotus, he should enter into meditative equipoise with her.

Having recited: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, the light rays from the seed-syllable at the heart summon the Tathāgatas, such as Vairocana, in union with their consorts, such as Locanā.

Having entered oneself through the gateway of Vairocana, one should imagine that those who have been melted by great passion proceed from the avadhūtī; then, the sahaja should be revealed at the vajra-jewel.

Having pressed the vajra-jewel with the thumb and the ring finger, one should resolve that those Tathāgatas who have emerged from the lotus and have melted are inseparable from one’s own bodhicitta; then, having seen the union of method and wisdom, and fearing lack of faith, one should bind the face with a veil for the disciples in the manner of the Vajra Speech.
Those who enter should be led in by the Yoginī holding the *karmavajra*. Having placed their knees on the ground and joined their palms together with flowers, they should say:
"O Blessed One, Great Peaceful One, solely devoted to Vajrayoga!
O Indestructible One who accomplishes the mudrās, arisen from Vajrayoga!"
O Lord, just as you are great-souled beings, do that for me as well;
I am submerged in the thick mire of saṃsāra—save me, who am without refuge.
Thus one should offer praise.

"O Blessed One, Great Peaceful One! O Vajrayoginī, who desires the singular [union], you who accomplish the indivisible mudrā, truly arisen from vajra-activity—just as you are of great selfhood, O Pervasive Lord, please make me likewise! Protect me, who am sinking without refuge within the mire of saṃsāra! With these words, one should offer praise to the guru.
Then the Guru, having risen, says:
"Just as the sons of the Buddha were sprinkled by Vajradhara and others in the past,
so do I sprinkle you, my child, with the beautiful bodhicitta."

Having thus recited the verses, and while reciting the mantra of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, *oṃ āḥ vajradhṛk hūṃ*, and so forth according to the tantra, he should pour [the water] into the mouth of the disciple.

Then the Guru rises and, preceded by the recitation of this verse: "Just as the Buddhas and their Sons were empowered by the past Vajradharas and others, so shall I empower you, my son, with the sublime bodhicitta," he proceeds.
One should cause [the mantra] to descend into the disciple's mouth by reciting the mantras of the lords of the mandala exactly as they are, beginning with *oṃ āḥ vajradhṛk hūṃ*.
He too, with the thought that it is the assembly of all the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana, should drink while saying, "Aho mahāsukham! (O, great bliss!).
He should drink while uttering, "Aṃ ho mahāsukhaṃ," [thinking] that it is the assembly of all the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana.

Having been thus instructed, she should rise up naked and place the drops of nectar from the Tathāgata situated upon her own lotus into his mouth; he too should drink in that same manner. Thus, through the secret initiation, there is the purification of speech.

Then, having also arisen through wisdom, one should place the drops of the Tathāgata’s nectar—which reside in the lotus fallen into a state of nakedness—into his mouth; he too should drink them in that same manner. This is the secret empowerment, which is the purification of speech.
Thereafter, [addressing] her or another woman who abides by the commitments and vows, and who is rich in beauty and youth:
"O Lord, by the grace of your feet, I have obtained the unsurpassed secret;
through the initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), grant me your favor."
To the disciple who had thus requested with this verse:
"This delightful dhāraṇī, revealed by the Buddhas, should be cultivated by you;
through the application of the sequence of the wheels, experience the true bliss."
"Seize, seize her, O Great Being—the goddess who bestows delight, who bestows a dwelling, who possesses universal form, and who is enchanting; having seized her, perform worship."
Having thus explained, one should offer [the gift].

Following that, whether it be she or another, a wisdom-consort (*prajñā*) who abides by the commitments (*samaya*) and the [yogic] practices—or alternatively, one endowed with beauty, youth, and so forth—[one should say]: "O Protector, through the grace of your feet, I have obtained the unsurpassed secret empowerment; now, through the wisdom-knowledge empowerment (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), please grant me your protection."

Having been thus requested with these verses, [the Master] says to the disciple: "The Buddhas have instructed that you should teach this delightful dhāraṇī. Through the application of the stages of the wheel, may you experience supreme bliss. O Great Being, take hold of, take hold of this goddess who bestows joy and bestows the state [of liberation], she who possesses various forms and is delightful."
Having made [them] understand thus, one should entrust [the teaching].

Then the Vidyā, O Beloved, having beheld the practitioner— dark-hued, naked, and adorned with flower ornaments— rises and, displaying clearly a fragrant lotus with the *pratyālīḍha* and other postures, with the gesture of raising the right foot, with the *maṇḍalapada* step, or in a squatting position (*utkuṭaka*), accompanied by the four *samādhis*, should joyfully say this: "O Child,
are you able to consume feces, urine, and so forth, as if they were food, O Beloved?"
"Blood, semen, and likewise flesh, as well as supreme devotion to women—
this is the method he would say.
Furthermore, O Goddess, I cannot bring myself to consume semen, blood, and the like."
Women should always practice devotion, as well as kissing and [the enjoyment of] the vulva.
Aho! My lotus is endowed with all happiness;
for whoever serves it according to the prescribed rite, I stand before them.
O Padmā, perform whatever tasks are required, such as the propitiation of the Perfectly Awakened One;
for the King of Great Bliss himself is always present right here.
One should say, "Devote yourself to liberation."
Then he too, having risen, kissed her face, embraced her, and sat down.

Then, the Vidyā also gazes at the practitioner like a goddess of desire; she stands up, adorned with flower ornaments though divested of her garments, and performs graceful gestures such as the extended left leg, as well as the postures of the extended right leg, the circular stance, and the squatting position.

Having made it fragrant with the four equalities and so forth, and having clearly displayed the lotus, one should joyfully utter this very [verse]: "O, this lotus of mine is the abode of all bliss! Whoever practices according to the ritual, before them I abide. Perform the activities of the Buddha’s teaching and so forth, exactly as they are upon the lotus."
The King of Great Bliss himself also constantly enters into this very state while reciting "bhanydza mokṣa hoḥ. Then, having arisen, one should embrace [the consort] with passion and remain in union.
Then the Guru should explain the distinctions of joy and so forth:
"Having placed the vajra in the lotus, one should not emit the bodhicitta."
Having stirred that bliss and filled the mind, one should meditate.
As long as the yogi, having generated [the consort], does not release the bodhicitta,
so long he attains an uninterrupted, indescribable bliss born of joy.
But when the bodhicitta, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen,
and the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, how can there be irreproachable accomplishment?

"From the union of the Vajra-realm and the Vajra, and from their contact, a great wonder arises; that bliss which is produced in the space-element (ākāśadhātu) brings about supreme joy. Thus it is said.

Having firmly placed the vajra upon the lotus, one should not emit the bodhicitta. Having moved it, one should cultivate the mind of joy and meditate upon it. As long as the yogin does not let the bodhicitta depart, he should maintain that uninterrupted flow of whatever joy and bliss have arisen. This is the support for all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).

"When the bodhicitta falls, the aggregate of consciousness becomes faint; how then could there be any accomplishment? Through the union of the space-realm and the vajra, there is a great and marvelous touch; whatever bliss arises from that is the creator of supreme joy. And: "In the lotus-space, at the point of pressing the excellent jewel-bud, one should gaze at the mind as it enters the jewel [tip] from the vajra-posture."
In the place where the seed-syllable of the Padma-jewel has arisen within the sky, one should visualize the mind abiding within that jewel in the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
Whatever cognition arises, that cognition is of that very form—enough of this!
Within the interval between the supreme and the cessation, having perceived the objective, make it firm. As for that which is within the food, that is the stainless form; [perceive it].
That wisdom which has definitely arisen is the stainless form; having observed its characteristics within the center of the supreme, joy-free, and pure, one should make it firm.

Thus, having realized the various forms of bliss through the grace of the Guru, one becomes oneself the embodiment of the deity. Having generated Prajñā in the form of the Goddess, one visualizes the filaments and jewels of the lotus and thunderbolt produced from *hrīḥ* and *hūṃ*, and within the mouth of the Vajra—produced from *āḥ* and *oṃ*—one contemplates a yellow *phaṭ*. Then, having moved the channel located in the left-left limb by means of the tongue and the forefinger marked with a red *hrīḥ* at its tip, preceded by the sound *śī*, one recites: *oṃ śī 2 ha 2 svāhā*.

Reciting the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, and with his body empowered by the Tathāgatas and others drawn forth by the rays from the seed-syllable in his own heart, he becomes of one flavor with the Guru who has introduced him and the infinite Vairocana-Locanā and so forth; thus, he should begin the act of delight.

By reciting "Anne śī 3 ha 3," through the guru’s grace, one generates oneself as the form of the deity and the consort as the form of the goddess, endowed with the distinctions of the various joys; then, from *hrīḥ* and *hūṃ*, the lotus and vajra arise, their pericarp and jewel generated from *āḥ* and *oṃ*.

One should clearly visualize a yellow syllable *phaṭ* at the tip of the vajra; likewise, a red syllable *hrīḥ* resides at the tips of the channel located on the left side, the index finger, and the tongue. Having been perfectly impelled by the preceding blue syllable *śī*, one recites: *oṃ śī śī śī śī ha ha ha svāhā*.

Reciting the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, one should invite the Tathāgatas and others through the light rays of the seed-syllable at one’s own heart and cause them to enter the body.
Then, as the master also causes Vairocana, Locanā, and the others to enter in immeasurable numbers, they become of one taste; thus, one should initiate the joy (*ānanda*).
When the yogi remains in bliss through the vision of gnosis, he does not fall away for a watch,
a day, a fortnight, a month, or even a year.

"One should remain for an eon or a thousand eons through application to primordial wisdom. Thus it is said: "When one perceives the yoga of primordial wisdom, one abides in bliss without change. For a watch, or a day and night, or for a fortnight, a month, or a year; for an eon or even a thousand eons, one should abide in the application of primordial wisdom. And: "Having placed the disciple within the heart of the lotus, one should release him."
Then, having observed the disciple, one should seize the mind with the tongue, preceded by the thought of awakening.
The disciple should take hold of its parts and cause them to expand within the lotus; then, with a mind that extracts the essence, she should first grasp enlightenment.
Thus, by means of the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge, there is the purification of the mind-vajra.
Thus, this is the empowerment of the primordial wisdom of insight; it is the activity of the Vajra Mind.
Thereafter,
through the initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka*), there is the purification of the mind-vajra.
Now, O Leader, may you inspire confidence in me even regarding the fourth [truth].
Through the empowerment of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), the vajra of the mind has been thoroughly purified; now, O Guide, please bestow upon me the fourth [empowerment] as well.

Thus, one should explain the reality—which was previously like darkness—to the disciple who has made such a request through words. According to the aforementioned procedures, the jewel-like consecration called the "Fourth," which is the fruit of having directly received the consecration of the Wisdom-Knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), must be declared; it is not for anyone else, due to the fear of violating the *samaya*. As the Blessed One said:
"Having bestowed the consecration according to the prescribed rites, one should examine the disciple’s inclination with the mind."
Or, for one who has faith in the noble and profound method, he should give the jewel of empowerment with words alone.

Thus, for the disciple who has made this request, the authentic reality (*tattva*) of the aforementioned meaning should be taught through words. Just as the empowerment of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka*) was directly apprehended through the spoken words, so too shall the fourth empowerment—the precious fruit—be explained.

Otherwise, the Blessed One has spoken of the fear of exhausting one’s commitments (*samaya*). Having bestowed the empowerment according to the ritual as it was taught, one should correctly examine the disciple’s inclination of mind. If they have superior devotion for the profound and vast system, that precious empowerment should be bestowed with these words:
And again: "Furthermore,
that yogi who, though not yet consecrated, desires the state of a yogi..."
He might as well strike the sky with his fist or drink from a mirage.
Without empowerment, the yogin is deceived regarding yoga itself; it is like punching the air with one's fist or drinking the thirst of a deer.
And in the Bodhisattva-vinaya: "Those who lack restraint do not attain liberation.
This means that in the Bodhisattva-vinaya as well, if one lacks the vows, one does not hold to liberation.
But how is it to be understood whether this person possesses noble resolve or not? To this it has been said:
"Is he one who eats or not? Fire is known by smoke, and water by the crane."
The lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known by its signs.
The wise one,
seeing that his excellent disciple has a lotus-face exceedingly serene and the hair on his body bristling with joy, favors him by [revealing] the reality as it truly is.

If one asks, "How then is it to be understood that this person has an exceptional inclination toward the vast [Mahāyāna]? it was said: Just as water is known from the presence of water-fowl, And fire is recognized from smoke, The lineage of the wise Bodhisattva Is known from its signs: An exceedingly bright face like a lotus, And a body from which joy overflows.
"Looking at that very [point], the wise one should take care of the excellent disciple. Thus it is said.
That has been stated in the Hevajra:
"That very [point] was also spoken in the Hevajra."
In this tantra, the consecration is established as divided into three types:
the master, the secret, and the wisdom; and the fourth is likewise that very same [consecration].
The three empowerments, inseparable, are established in this tantra: the master, the secret, the wisdom, and likewise the fourth.
The attainment of laughter, gazing, and the hand occurs in that dual mantra;
in the dual tantra,
there the master [is attained] through the purification of laughter, and the secret one likewise through gazing.
Laughing for an instant and touching with the hand, as well as embracing, arise from the Tantra; laughing is the state of the Ācārya, and looking is likewise the Secret [Initiation].
And when wisdom has attained its hand, that [skill] is again applied in the union of the pair.
In the *Dvandvatantra*:
"Bliss (*ānanda*), supreme bliss (*parama*), the cessation (*virama*), and likewise the innate (*sahaja*).
In the [same] *Sahaja* [tantra]: "The innate."
From holding hands comes wisdom itself; that also arises from the mutual embrace of the two. Joy, supreme joy, the joy beyond joy, and likewise the innate joy—these are they.
The diverse, the ripening, the dissolution, and the distinct.
Through the sequence of consecrations, all ritual procedures arise from union with the limb of wisdom.
Know that food is manifold, ripened, and likewise liberated from characteristics; all the rituals of the sequence of mastery arise from attachment to the branches of wisdom.
Through *ānanda* there is some pleasure; *paramānanda* is greater than that;
*viramānanda* would be the absence of passion (*virāga*); and *sahajānanda* remains as the remainder.
A slight bliss of joy arises; supreme joy is greater than that; the absence of joy is the state free from attachment; the remainder becomes innate joy.
The first [desire] is a longing for touch; the second is due to a wish for pleasure;
the third is due to the destruction of passion; by the fourth, nothing is produced.
The first is the desire for touch; the second is the desire for pleasure; the third is the fear of passion itself; thereafter, one should cultivate the fourth.
In the *vicitra* stage there is the first bliss (*prathamānanda*); supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) is in the *vipāka*;
the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*) is in the *vimarda*; and innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is in the *vilakṣaṇa*.
The manifold is the joy of the first; the ripened is the supreme joy; the vanished is the joy free from joy; and that which is devoid of characteristics is innate joy itself.
The "variegated" (vicitra) is known as the manifold [practices] such as embracing, kissing, and so forth;
the "ripening" (vipāka) is the reverse of that, which is the enjoyment of bliss and gnosis.
Embracing, kissing, and so forth—these various and manifold forms are described; the ripening [result] is the reverse of those, which is the practice of the wisdom of perfect bliss.
Vimarda is said to be reflection, such as thinking, "I have experienced pleasure";
Vilakṣaṇa is other than those three, being free from both passion and dispassion.

It is taught that one's own clothing should be worn until it is completely worn out; for those who are free from characteristics, they have utterly abandoned both attachment and detachment toward others.
Therefore, it is said:
"For that very reason, it is stated:
'Neither passion nor dispassion, nor the middle, is perceived.'"
Precisely through the avoidance of these three, it is called innate awakening.
It is neither passion nor free from passion; it is not perceived as a middle way. Because these three have been abandoned, it is called innate awakening.
This was stated by Kṛṣṇapāda.
From the union of the lotus and the vajra, there arises this diverse ripening in contact and so forth;
subsequently, the fire of passion arising from churning consumes the world, while the friction of the battle-sword crushes it.
Having meditated upon that wind within the mind, in the lotus that accompanies the fire of passion—
This very path to perfect enlightenment is the body of all the Victors, accessible to yogins, and free from defining characteristics.

The various [sensations] such as pleasure and so forth are the maturation (*vipāka*); that which abides as the vajra within the lotus is the ripened result. Subsequently, having been incinerated by the fire of passion born from churning, the aggregates attached to the guest [the sense objects] are destroyed. Therein, the mind grasps while the winds function together; in the water-born [lotus], the fire becomes predominant.
This is the path to perfect enlightenment; the entire body of the Victorious One is the goal of yoga, free from characteristics.
It has also been said by the daughters:
Āryakapāda also said:
"The mind, consisting of mere bliss, spreads out at the base of the jewel; then again, it is restless with all its conceptual constructions in the middle of the jewel."
Above that, at the peak of the summit, something peaceful, of the nature of the cloudless sky, spontaneously arisen and seated upon a lotus, expands. || 145 ||

The food [is] situated upon the lotus; it is merely the manifold bliss (*vicitrānanda*) firmly established at the base of the jewel. Furthermore, the remainder is within the center of the jewel, accompanied by conceptualization and movement. Above that, the *ūrdhvaretas* (upward-flowing vital essence) drips from the crown of the head; it is the form of the immovable, the co-emergent (*sahaja*) residing in the mud-born [lotus], the Buddha. What other activity could there be?
It was also said by Virūpapāda: [In the Tibetan version:
"Also spoken by the one called Virūpa"].
As long as the flow of the cool-rayed moon, consisting of radiant light, does not fall within the interior of the petals of the Goddess’s lotus— having become one in flavor with the hosts of Victors—
[so long shall] the cause of the world remain unbroken by compassion from the tip of the throbbing vajra-peak.
Know that to be the innate form of the Lord, whose power is glorious compassion.
O Rāmapāla! O Munidatta (ascribed to the *Sekoddeśa*)!

Just as the cool-rayed moon does not fall from the sky, so too the hosts of Victors, having attained equal taste within the petals of the lotus of the consort, radiate from the tip of the vajra-forehead; they perform deeds for beings with indivisible compassion.
To whatever extent the power of glorious compassion is coemergent, it is the form that pervades all that is knowable.
Indrabhūtipāda also said:
"As long as [the drop] is unstable and falls due to the wind into the fire of the three vajras within the vajra-jewel..."
At this moment, the mind— devoid of conceptual constructions such as self and other, and free from activity— dwells within the hollow chamber of the lotus-heart, desiring to remain there;
we know that this very innate state is indeed made manifest once more through reasoning and scripture.
O Rāmapāla, know this!

As long as the three vajras are being incinerated and shaken by the wind of the moon within the navel of the lotus-abode, one should remain firm in this state called "the desire to enter. Therein, one is free from conceptualizations such as self and other; all activities are of an inferior mind.
It should be understood that innate suchness is clearly realized once again.
Moreover:
Neither at its root, nor in its stalk, nor in the space between its petals does the lotus possess form.
"O Śaṅkha, you are by nature different; you will go to the abode of Vajrasimha, and not until then [will this end]," and so forth.

"It is not the root of that, nor is it the heart; it is not without the application of the lotus, yet as long as there is no movement from the vajra-tip, so long is it the innate characteristic, being devoid of [dualistic] characteristics," and so forth.
This very same meaning is also stated in the *Śrī-samāja*.
That which is the union of the goal and the means is called "sādhana" (the practice);
the union of the vajra and the lotus is called "upasādhana" (the near-practice).
The practice (sādhana) is said to be the movement accompanied by the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*;
the great practice (mahāsādhana) is called one's own nature, which is blissful and peaceful.

This very point was also taught in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*: "The authentic union of the object to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment—whatever is spoken of as 'accomplishment' (*sādhana*)—the equal conjunction of the vajra and the lotus is called 'near-accomplishment' (*upasādhana*). Possessing the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, it is said to be 'movement' during the stage of accomplishment (*sādhana*). That which is blissful by its very nature is called 'great accomplishment' (*mahāsādhana*)."

Wisdom is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and means (*upāya*) is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Their union is *sevā*; the entry of the vajra into the lotus is *upasādhana*; the movement [of the vital energy] is *sādhana*; and one's own nature, which is peaceful with its own bliss, is called *mahāsādhana*.

The object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is method (*upāya*); their perfect union is *sevā*. The entry of the vajra into the lotus is *upasādhana*. Movement is *sādhana*. Being blissful and peaceful by its very nature is taught as *mahāsādhana*.

Joy (*ānanda*) lasts until the vajra-entry of the means and the goal; supreme joy (*paramānanda*) lasts until the extreme movement of the bodhicitta; cessation joy (*viramānanda*) is the emission; and when one's own bliss becomes peaceful in the interval between these two, that is innate joy (*sahajānanda*).

The object of accomplishment and the means of accomplishment are the ultimate joy (*paramānanda*) when the vajra has fully entered; the supreme joy (*viramānanda*) occurs at the end of the bodhicitta that is intensely stirred; the joy of separation (*viramānanda*) occurs at the moment of emission. When one abides in a state of self-bliss and tranquility between these [stages], that is called the innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
That has been stated in the Hevajra:
"In that very [reality] taught in the glorious Hevajra,
there is neither existence nor nirvāṇa at the beginning, the end, or the middle."
This is that supreme great bliss; it is neither another nor the self.
Now, it is neither beginning, middle, nor end; it is neither existence nor nirvāṇa. This is supreme great bliss; it is not other, nor is it not other.
Existence is said to be supreme bliss, and nirvāṇa is from the absence of passion;
but the innate (sahaja) is devoid of these, being merely the intermediate bliss.
Supreme joy is said to be existence; from the absence of joy comes nirvāṇa. That which is merely joy is the middle way; by this, even the innate is abandoned.
When supreme bliss has been attained in the moment devoid of multiplicity,
and when that supreme bliss has indeed been reached,
the Teacher should say: "O Great Being, this is the great bliss to be maintained."
O Vajradhara, act for the benefit of sentient beings until the very limit of enlightenment.
And so forth, in detail.

"Through supreme joy one attains [the state] in the moment when variety is abandoned; the Great Being spoken of by the Teacher—grasp this great bliss! As long as enlightenment is not reached, you shall be a Vajradhara for the sake of sentient beings," and so on, extensively.
[Then] how is it that it was stated [previously] that it is divided into three kinds?
If one asks how those three aspects are taught to be inseparable:
"Because there is no difference between cause and fruit, it was previously proclaimed as threefold;
because of its luminosity between the joys of cessation (*viramānanda*) [and the preceding joy], it is fourfold."
Because the fruit is not other than the cause, it is renowned as being threefold; [it is so designated] because the fourth is excluded from within the midst of joy and the absence of joy.
If it is asked: "But how is it that luminosity is explained as being between these two?"
It is said: because of the statement, "The supreme limit is the cessation of the middle; Heruka, however, is both empty and non-empty."
From the statement: "The supreme limit and the center free from joy; emptiness and non-emptiness, Heruka."
How is it that [it is called] "empty" or "non-empty"?
Regarding the question "How is it empty or non-empty?":
It is the Lord who is without beginning or end, peaceful, and whose nature consists of both existence and non-existence.
O Mother, the all-pervading, indivisible unity of emptiness and compassion is known as bodhicitta.
This is because of the established tenet [which states]:

"That which is peaceful, without beginning or end, the sovereign whose nature is both existence and non-existence, and inseparable from compassion itself—this is what is called 'bodhicitta,'" as found in the *Siddhānta*.
By what means is this to be generated?
By means of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, and indeed by the stage of self-consecration.
One should generate the thought of awakening, which consists of both the ultimate and the conventional aspects.
Through the method of the maṇḍala wheel and the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), one should generate the bodhicitta, which possesses the forms of both the conventional and the ultimate.
And this cannot be expressed by words. Why? Because:
"These cannot be expressed by anyone; for what reason?
This knowledge is self-cognized, its domain transcending the path of speech."
For this is the sequence of self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), which consists of the wisdom of the Omniscient One.

This wisdom of individual self-cognition is the sphere of experience that transcends the activities of the [ordinary] elements; through this stage of self-consecration, the nature of that omniscient wisdom [is realized].
The innate is not described by another, nor is it found in anyone else;
it is known by oneself through merit and by serving the lineage of gurus.
The co-emergent cannot be expressed by another; it is not found anywhere. It is to be known through attending to the succession of gurus and from one's own merit.
By the grace of the Guru's feet, knowledge that transcends the path of speech arises instantaneously of its own accord in those of great merit.
Through the grace of the Guru’s speech and by virtue of one's own great merit, the wisdom of the karma of retention is a sphere of experience that transcends the path of words.
Thus it was said:
"Victorious is the unique King of Bliss, devoid of causes, eternally arisen for all worlds."
And at the time of whose description, even the Omniscient One became impoverished of words.
May the sole King of Bliss prevail—he who, when being expressed, leaves even the Omniscient One lacking words; he who is eternally manifest to beings who are free from agency. Saraha-pāda also said:
[Saraha-pāda also said:]
The Guru does not speak of that to the disciple, nor is that understood by the disciple; for whom and why should this nectar-like state of innate being be told?

The reality of that [is realized] through the speech of the Guru; it is realized by the Guru himself. How could the taste of the nectar of the coemergent state ever be described, and how could it be known?
And again:
Since it is beyond the range of the intellect, it does not fall within the sphere of speech.
The introduction to the discourse on the most renowned and profound subject is far off;
yet, that [subject] gradually establishes its own footing in the hearts of those possessed of faith, which have been purified by virtues such as compassion.

This is not within the sphere of the intellect and lies far beyond the reach of words; it is devoid of the discourse on the reality of gurus. Yet, through the sequence of the tantras, it causes qualities such as compassion to arise, bestowing the state of realization upon the heart that possesses natural clarity.
Now, what is the characteristic of one who has generated the mind of awakening? That is stated:
The sense faculties seem to fall asleep, and the mind seems to enter within.
The body appears as if its movements have ceased, being fainting from true bliss.
The sense faculties are as if in their own natural state; the mind is as if withdrawn within; the speech is as if faltering; and the body is perfectly suffused with bliss.
With senses withdrawn, free from conceptual construction, and with the seeds of existence not yet exhausted, he consists of bliss; though equal to space, oh, how cool and sweet he is!
The collection of faculties has perished and no longer functions; conceptualization is incomplete, the seed of existence. This nature of joy is like the cooling experience of a flower in the sky.
O friend, ask the feet of the Guru about that body which is innate bliss, wherein the intellect has dissolved and its own nature is lost.

The path of the senses has become utterly stilled; whatever its nature may be when it has thus declined, its fruit is a singular joy. Ask this of the Teacher’s own mouth, as if from a flower upon his body.
This very point is stated:
"Homage to him, simultaneously with whose arising..."
The sense-faculties have set along with their objects;
and he whose beautiful form is like that of a victorious Buddha remains alone, yet awake, silently within the hearts of the wise.

I prostrate to him who, by his arising, causes time to perish and abides upon the crown of the head, whose object and sense faculty are identical. Furthermore, may this single, beautiful body of the Victorious One, Abhirati, awaken within the hearts of the wise and remain there.
And again:
"He whose intellect, having all conceptual constructions obstructed, moves here toward true happiness."
And he, the wise one who has accomplished what was to be done, is distinct from those others who are mere beasts among bipeds.
Thus, enough with this elaboration.

When the conceptual constructions of the mind have been utterly destroyed, that which here empowers sublime bliss—this task should be performed by the wise. Furthermore, [it is said]: "Possessing the intention for excellence," and so forth, at length.
Therefore, having propitiated a truly authentic guru, good disciples must personally realize the nature of great bliss (mahāsukha) that exists within the three bodies.
Therefore, the excellent disciple should show reverence to the authentic, sublime guru, and one should personally realize the great bliss of entering the three.

Immediately thereafter, having placed the hand of that Prajñā into the hand of the disciple and bound them together with a garland of flowers, and holding those two with his own left hand, he places his right hand, which holds a vajra, upon the disciple’s head in front of the maṇḍala.

Immediately following that, the Wisdom Consort places her hand into the hand of the disciple and binds a garland of flowers upon him. Holding both of them with her own left hand, she places her right hand—joined with a vajra—upon the head of the disciple. Then, in front of the mandala, she calls upon the Tathāgatas as witnesses, saying: "You are the witnesses here; I have now entrusted this [disciple] to him."
"Here you are the masters; I entrust this to you," thus the Tathāgatas have made [the disciple] their master.
"Since there is no other means for Buddhahood and these three worlds are pure, therefore, never be separated from her."
This is that unsurpassed vidyā-vow of all the Buddhas;
for the fool who transgresses it, there shall be no supreme accomplishment.

There is no Buddhahood through any other means, nor is this triple world real; therefore, you must never be separated from this. This is the unsurpassed observance of the *vidyā* of all Buddhas; for any fool who transgresses it, there will be no supreme siddhi.
Saying this, he should cause him to receive the vow of knowledge (vidyāvrata).
Having spoken thus, one should undertake the observance of the Vidyā; this is the ritual procedure for bestowing the Vidyā-vow.
This is the ritual for the gift of the observance of the vidyā.
Then, having visualized the disciple in the form of Vajrasattva:
"This is that state of all Buddhas, which resides in the hand of Vajrasattva;
