you too must always uphold it, O Vajrapāṇi of firm vows."

Reciting thus, one should place the vajra in the right hand. The mantra is: *oṃ sarvatathāgata siddhi vajrasamaya tiṣṭha eṣa tvāṃ dhārayāmi vajrasattva hrīḥ hi hi hi hi hūṃ*. Reciting this, one should take hold of it; this is the procedure for the vajra-vow (*vajravratavidhi*).

Then, having visualized the disciple in the form of Vajrasattva, one says: "This is the state of all Buddhas; it resides in the hand of Vajrasattva. You too must always hold it, firm in the vow of Vajrapāṇi. Having spoken thus, one places the vajra in the right hand, and he [the disciple] likewise—

"oṃ sarvatathāgatasiddhivajrasamayetiṣṭha eṣa tvāṃ dhārayāmi vajrasattva hi hi hi hi hūṃ"—reciting this, one should grasp [the vajra]. This is the ritual for bestowing the vajra-vow (vajravratadānavidhi).
Then, having recited three times over the *khaṭvāṅga*,
the *ḍamaru*, and the lotus vessel with the heart mantra of any one of the deities such as Buddhakapāla,
Saṃvara, or Hevajra: "O Hero, take this *khaṭvāṅga*, the *ḍamaru*, and the bowl, which have been offered."
Therefore, this mudrā of Śrī Vajrasattva, which abides both externally and internally, has been bestowed; thus it is established.
This mudrā of Vajrasattva abides perfectly both externally and internally; thereafter, with the syllables Kha, Tvam, Caṅ, and Te’u, the hero should grasp the vessel as an offering.
Reciting this verse, one should cause [the disciple] to memorize it.

Alternatively, as stated in other tantras, one should cause them to take up another limb of conduct, such as the khaṭvāṅga and so forth— consecrated by the heart-mantra of the respective Lord of the Mandala— with the words, "Take [this]," and so on.

Furthermore, regarding those ancillaries of conduct taught in the *Kha-tvā-ga-la* and other tantras, one should recite them with the essence mantra of the Lord of the Wheel of that [deity], and cause them to be maintained by means of the words beginning with "Vajrasattva."
And likewise, in the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*: "Thus also, from the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*..."
One should fashion a great image, white in color, wearing a crown of matted locks, in accordance with the ritual rules, entirely conforming to the vows and commitments of the mantra.
One should partake of all food and edibles consisting of bulbs, roots, and fruits.

The form of the one who wears the crown, standing upright, is great like the color white; everything should be performed according to the ritual, perfectly purified through the meditation on the mantra. One should enjoy the stalks, roots, and fruits equally as all forms of sensory experience.
By these and other such statements, the *caryāvratam* (vow of conduct) has been explained for the purpose of undertaking the *vidyāvrata* (vow of knowledge).
By these and other such statements, it is taught that one should undertake the observance of the *vidyā* vow and perform the conduct of that vow.

As for the woman or man who requests the observance of the *caryā-vrata*, one should visualize her in the form of Nairātmyā or Vajravārāhī, or in the form of whichever Family Goddess corresponds to the falling of the flower; and the man as the form of Saṃvara, Hevajra, or another deity. Then, having caused the Wisdom Deity—summoned by rays of light from the seed-syllable in the heart of that [deity]—to enter into her or him.

Furthermore, whether it be a queen or a man observing the ascetic discipline (*vrata*), one should visualize them in the form of Vajravārāhī or Nairātmyā, or in the form of the deity of the family corresponding to the fall of the flower; and for men, in the form of any suitable deity such as Saṃvara or Hevajra.
Then, having caused the wisdom deities (*jñānadeva*)—summoned by the light rays of the seed-syllable at the heart—to enter into each of them, one should [proceed].
Akṣobhya is in the form of the wheel, Amitābha is the nature of the earring,
Ratneśa is in the necklace around the neck, and Vairocana is said to be in the hand.
One should place Amoghasiddhi on the girdle, Vajradhṛk on all the limbs;

Akṣobhya in the form of the earrings, Amitābha as the nature of the necklace, Ratneśa on the neck-garland, Rūpacandra (Vairocana) mindful of the bracelets, Amoghasiddhi residing on the sash, and Vajradhṛk on all the members.

Having spoken thus, one should instantly visualize—in due order—the wheel, earrings, necklace, bracelets, girdle, and ashes as being the forms of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasaṃbhava, Vairocana, Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva. Then, having caused the respective Jñānasattvas brought from that [pure realm] to enter those [seals], one should resolve with conviction that the seals, such as the wheel and so forth, which have been transformed into Akṣobhya and the others, are indeed of the very nature of Akṣobhya and the rest.

Having recited three times: *oṃ dhara dhara dhāraya dhāraya marda marda vajradhṛk phaṭ svāhā*, one should place the wheel upon his or her head while reciting the verse beginning with "Take it," substituting "Vīra" for "Devī" in the case of a female. Having recited three times: *oṃ vajradharma samayas tvaṃ kuru hulu ārolik phaṭ svāhā*, one should place the two earrings on the ears.

"Oṃ vajrasūrya tamovidhamāna [or °vidhūnana] samayas tvam ahaṃ ratnadhṛk phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this three times, he places the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*) upon his neck. "Oṃ śāśvata paramaśāśvata ehy ehi jinajik phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this three times, he places the two bracelets (*rucaka*) on his hands like bangles.

Having recited "Oṃ phu 2 hi 2 prajñādhṛk phaṭ svāhā" three times over the girdle, one should subsequently address it as "O Goddess" or "O Heroine" according to the sequence, and then recite: "The discus is the form of Akṣobhya," "the two earrings are Vāgvajra," "the necklace is Ratnasaṃbhava," "the bracelet is the nature of Śāśvata," and "the girdle is Amoghasiddhi. Having thus projected these, one should recite "Take [it]," and so forth.

Having spoken thus, one should instantly visualize, in their respective order, the wheel, earrings, necklace, bracelets, belt, and ashes as the forms of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasambhava, Vairocana, Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva.

Having likewise inserted the clear eyes of that and its wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*), one should cultivate firm conviction (*adhimukti*) that the hand-symbols such as the wheel, which have arisen from the complete transformation of Akṣobhya and the others, are the very nature of Akṣobhya and so forth, reciting: *oṃ dhara dhara dhāraya dhāraya marda marda vajradhṛk phaṭ svāhā*.

Having recited this three times, one should place that wheel at the head [of each] with the verse beginning "Vajrasattva," and so forth. For the female side, one should substitute the word "goddess" (*devī*) for "hero" (*vīra*) and recite it as such. Oṃ vajradharma samayas tvam hulu hulu ārolik phaṭ svāhā.

Reciting this three times, the two ear-ornaments are for the ears. *Oṃ vajrasūryatamo buddhamanasamaya stvam ā ratna dhṛka phaṭ svāhā*. Reciting this three times, the necklace-ornament is for the neck. *Oṃ śāśvataparamaśāśvata ehyehi jinañjika phaṭ svāhā*.

The two bracelets, over which the mantra *oṃ phuḥ phuḥ hi hi hi prajñādhṛka phaṭ svāhā* has been recited three times, are for the hands like armlets. The girdle, over which the same mantra has been recited three times, is for the waist. Following the words "perfectly established," in the proper sequence: the wheel is the form of Akṣobhya, and the two earrings are Vāgvajra.

Thus it is said; and "the necklace is Ratnasambhava"; and "the bracelet is the nature of Nityanātha"; and "the girdle is Amoghasiddhi"—having inserted these, one should recite "Vajrasattva," and so forth.

Reciting "Oṃ Vajrasattva Hūṃ" three times, one should apply the ashes to all the limbs. For women, there is the wearing of the five mudrās without ashes; for men, however, there are six mudrās together with the ashes.
Reciting "oṃ vajrastvaṃ hūṃ" three times, one should apply the ashes to all the limbs. Women should hold the mudrā free from ashes, whereas men [should hold] the six mudrās together with the ashes.

However, if a woman or a man who has attained the capacity for the [four] visions and so forth wishes to undertake the vow of the Hero’s Conduct (*vīracaryāvrata*) for the sake of others, one should visualize her in the form of Vajravārāhī and him in the form of Saṃvara, as being of one flavor with the Jñānasattva. Having resolved that the wheel and other ornaments are as before, and that the garland of severed heads and so forth are the nature of their respective mantra-deities, one should recite "Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā" three times and place the wheel upon her in the same manner.

Furthermore, if any woman, having attained the power of the gaze and so forth of a man, desires to undertake the heroic conduct (*vīravratam*) for the sake of others, she should visualize herself as the form of Vajravārāhī and the form of Saṃvara as being of one taste with the *jñānasattva*; then, she should cultivate conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the wheel and the other [limbs] as before.

One should visualize the garland of heads and so forth as having the nature of the deity through their respective mantras; having recited "Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" three times, one should likewise meditate upon the wheel and the other [implements].

There are also five skull-cups consisting of the nature of the five Buddhas, as it is said: "The mantra 'Vairocani' is that which adorns the head with a skull. Here, the skull-cup is also in the form of a discus (*cakrī*). "Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ phaṭ"—recited three times, this is for the two earrings. As it is said: "With the seven-syllable mantra, the earring is the ornament of the ear. Or, with the root mantra of Vajravārāhī, or with the mantra beginning "Oṃ sarvabuddha... and so forth, recited three times, this is for the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*). As it is said:

Regarding the mantra of Vajravārāhī, which adorns the neck as a necklace (*kaṇṭhika*), it is: *oṃ haḥ namaḥ hi svāhā hūṃ vauṣaṭ he hūṃ hūṃ ho phaṭ 2 hūṃ*. Recited three times, this constitutes the two bracelets (*rucaka*). As it is said: "With these six [syllables] of the Armor (*kavaca*), this mudrā beautifies the limbs of the Hero. Regarding the girdle (*mekhalā*), it is: *oṃ vaṃ hāṃ yoṃ hrīṃ moṃ hreṃ hrīṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ 2*. Recited three times, this is the girdle. As it is said: "The ornament made of the girdle is formed by the mantra of the Six Yoginīs."

There is also the skull that is the nature of the five Buddhas; it is that which is called the *vairocana* mantra. As it is said: "The head is adorned with a skull. Here, the skull is also in the form of a wheel. With the mantra *oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, recited three times, there are two earrings; by means of this seven-syllable secret mantra, the ears are beautified with earrings.

Thus it was said. Regarding the root mantra of Vajravārāhī, or the mantra beginning with *oṃ sarvabuddha* and so forth, which is recited three times as a necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*): "Whatever is the mantra of Vajravārāhī, it adorns the throat as a necklace," as it was said. *oṃ haḥ | nama hi | svāhā hu | bhoḥ śada he | hūṃ hūṃ ho phaṭ haṃ*.

Thus, the two bracelets are recited three times; these six heroic armors are beautiful upon the body of this mudrā. The girdle is recited three times with "hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ," and the girdle is adorned as an ornament with the mantra of the six yoginīs, as it has been taught.

"Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru ka hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvaraṃ svāhā. Having recited this three times, one places a garland of fifty severed heads around the neck. As it is said: "The heart-mantra of the deity is indeed the garland adorned with fifty [heads]. "Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this three times, one puts on a tiger-skin garment. As it is said:

"Of all the Buddhas, the ḍākinīs wear garments of skin as supreme. With the mantras beginning with *oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* and ending with *oṃ rūpiṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, one recites these thirty-six mantras three times over the vessel for drinking the mantra-filled [substance], which is endowed with the characteristics to be described hereafter, and places it in the hand. As it is said: "The yoginīs of the entire maṇḍala hold skull-cups filled with mantra in their hands. Then, having consecrated the khaṭvāṅga and the ḍamaru three times with the root mantra of the Blessed One, beginning with *bhagavate vīreśāya* and so forth, one takes them up with the verse beginning with *gṛhṇe*.

*oṃ śrī vajra he heruka hūṃ phaṭ dākinījālasaṃvara svāhā*. Recite this three times. As for the garland of fifty human heads for the recitation, it is worn around the neck, as it is said: "Adorned with a garland of fifty [heads], the deity’s heart mantra serves as the necklace."

*oṃ sarvabuddhadākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. Reciting this three times, one takes a tiger skin for the purpose of a lower garment (*śamthabs*), as it is said: "The ḍākinīs of all Buddhas hold the supreme garment of skin. *oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, and so forth.

Recite the thirty-six mantras ending with *oṃ rūpiṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* three times. Then, using the mantra characterized by what will be explained later, it is said: "The vessel full [of wine] is held in the hand; it is the skull-cup for drinking, belonging to the Yoginīs of all the wheels. [The instruments are] the *kāhala*, the *damaru*, and...
Having praised three times with the root mantra of the Blessed One, *namo bhagavate vāreśaya*, by means of the verses beginning with Vajrasattva and so forth.

Again, with that same mantra, having recited it three times, one should place the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), the necklace suspended from the neck, the vajra-ornament, the crown made of thieves’ hair, the double-wrapped hair-braids, the ashes, the armlets, the anklets, and the *ghurghurā* bells each in their respective places. As it is said: "That which is the hero of the root mantra is fashioned as the sacred thread and so forth. Then, the sacred thread should be made with a single string, and the girdle with eight strings.

That same [string] around a woman’s waist consists of sixteen [strings], while a *hāra* consists of twenty-five. As it has been said: "A single-stringed cord is a *sūtra*; a *mekhalā* has eight strings; a *rasanā* is known to have sixteen; and a *mālin* has twenty-five."

Furthermore, with that same mantra, one should place the *brahmasūtra* recited three times, the necklace hanging from the neck, the vajra ornaments, the crown made of dacoit hair, the double-stranded waistband, the ashes, the armlets, the anklets, and the earrings each in their respective locations.

As it is said: "By means of the root mantra of the Hero, one should designate the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) and so forth. In that regard, a single string constitutes the sacred thread; eight strings constitute the waistband, which for women consists of sixteen; twenty-five strings constitute the necklace. Furthermore, a single string is the sacred thread.
"The waistband itself consists of eight strands; it should be understood as sixteen women. It is said to possess a garland of twenty-five."

Alternatively, the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) may be made of human bone or hair. Here, the wheel and other ornaments are appropriately fashioned from human bone, as are the vajras for the jewelry. One of these is worn on the topknot. As it has been said: "Having fashioned a skull-fragment five finger-breadths in size, it is always worn upon the crown. This very vow of the Hero’s Conduct (*vīracaryāvratam*) is called the vow-conduct of the Crown Prince (*yauvarājyavratacaryā*), and is also termed the "Vow-Conduct of the Vajra-Kāpālika," as stated in the *Śrīsampuṭatantra*. [The reading *vajrakapālicaryā* is preferred.]

Alternatively, there is a brahminical thread (*brahmasūtra*) made from human sinew or hair. Here, the ornaments such as the wheel and the vajra are appropriately made from human bone. Among these, one is worn on the crown of the head; as it is said: "One wears a crown fashioned from thirty-five fragments of a skull."

In the *Śrī Saṃpuṭa Tantra*, the very conduct of the heroic observance (*vīracaryāvrata*) is also taught as the "conduct of the youthful prince's observance" and the "observance of the Vajra Skull-bearer."
Thereafter, one should constantly worship with the five mudrās and so forth. This is the ritual for the bestowal of the conduct vow (*caryāvratadānavidhi*).
Thus concludes the ritual for the gift of the ascetic observances of conduct.
Then, having raised his hand, the excellent preceptor, himself becoming the Tathāgata, should explain [the initiation] to the disciple who is of the nature of Vajradhara.
Then the Guru, the Supreme Giver, shall grant the authentic empowerment of the mudrā; having become a Tathāgata himself, he [confers it upon] the disciple who is the very nature of a Vajradhara.
Making the gesture of offering a robe with the left hand and holding the boon-granting mudrā with the right,
he should recite this verse together with all the Tathāgatas:
Holding the religious robe with the left hand and displaying the gesture of supreme generosity with the right, one should recite this very verse together with all the Tathāgatas:
I, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, prophesy for you,
having extracted you from the miserable states of existence, for the sake of the ultimate pacification of cyclic existence.

Since you have been extracted from the miserable rebirths of existence, so that the very end of existence may be fully accomplished, I, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, shall grant you the prophecy you request.

Reciting the mantra *siddhya samayas tvaṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, the preceptor should confer the prophecy upon the disciple, saying: "O, you named [Name] Vajra Tathāgata, *siddhya samayas tvaṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. Whoever is thus prophesied is prophesied by all the Tathāgatas with a single voice for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, regarding this teaching, all the Tathāgatas bestow the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening with one voice;
such is the procedure for the prophecy.
Thus concludes the ritual for the prophecy.
These— namely, the knowledge, vajra, conduct, and vow empowerments— are in some tantras and similar works designated as "initiations" (*abhiṣeka*).
In certain tantras and other works, these—namely, the consort (*vidyā*), the vajra, the conduct-vow (*caryāvrata*), and the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*)—are designated as "empowerment" (*abhiṣeka*) itself.
Thereafter, having meditated on the disciple in the form of Vairocana or another [deity], in front of that seat—
with a wheel, a jewel, a lotus, or a vajra—
Then he should grant permission and recite this verse:
Likewise, bestow those permissions for the precious wheel, the lotus, and the vajra; recite these verses.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, toward all beings in every way,
turn the wheel of Dharma for the universe according to their respective dispositions.
For the benefit of all sentient beings, you have thoroughly turned the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings in every way, according to their various means of discipline.

Victory! Victory! O Lord of all Tathāgatas, turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, everywhere and in all worlds! *Jaya jaya sarvatathāgatādhipate pravartaya dharmacakraṃ sarvasattvahitārthāya sarvalokeṣu sarvataḥ*.
Reveal the jewel of the Buddha to the world according to the discipline.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, he perfectly displays the precious Buddha, in whatever various ways are necessary to discipline them.
Oṃ vajraratna, you who have obtained the empowerment of the pure wisdom of all phenomena, oṃ oṃ oṃ.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way,
manifest the purification of passion for the entire universe according to their respective dispositions.
For the benefit of all sentient beings, throughout the entire world and in every way, he perfectly demonstrates the purification of desire according to the various means of training.

Oṃ vajradharma sarvadharmaviśuddhajñānarāgapadmadalasvabhāva hrīḥ āḥ! Oṃ vajradharmaviśuddhajñānarāgapadmadalasvabhāvavajri āḥ! For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way.
In accordance with the Vinaya, perform the Vajra worship for the sake of the universe.
For the benefit of all sentient beings, throughout the entire world and in every way, perform the vajra offering that accords with the various means of conversion.
Oṃ vajrakarma-sarvadharma-viśuddha-jñāna-pūjā-svabhāva āḥ! Furthermore, in order to grant the special permission (*viśeṣānujñā*):
Furthermore, the special permission (viśeṣānujñā) should be granted as follows:

while reciting "Oṃ vajrabhāṣe raṃ," one places a conch shell born from the syllable ĀḤ in the left hand; then, while reciting the final vowel, one gives a bell born from the final vowel. [The preceptor then addresses] the disciple who is sounding that bell.

Reciting "oṃ vajrabhāṣaṇa," [the preceptor] gives a conch born from the syllable *ā* and, while reciting the final vowel, a bell born from the final vowel, into the left hand. Then, having the disciple ring the bell, [he says]:
"All things have the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics.
Through the union with the equality of space, the equality of all that is supreme is made manifest."
All things have the characteristic of space, and space itself has no characteristic; through union with the equality of space, the supreme of all is revealed as equality.
"From this day forward, by the mere arising of the thought [of awakening], turn the wheel of Dharma;
for you have completely filled the unsurpassed conch of Dharma in every direction."
"From this moment forth, by the mere generation of the mind endowed with faith, you shall turn the wheel of Dharma and completely fill the unsurpassed conch of Dharma. Thus it is said.
And again:
one should then offer a vessel fashioned and adorned with the seven precious gems.
A knife, a chisel, chalk, a rosary, and a book.
The great mantra-practitioner, with a most exalted mind, should bestow upon him an alms-bowl, a lotus, a pair of sandals, and a meditation belt.

One should bestow the seven precious jewels fashioned from various materials. At the conclusion of reciting: "The curved knife (*kartṛkā*), the *khaṭvāṅga*, the rosary, the book, the dice, the yogic staff (*yogadaṇḍa*)," that great mantra-practitioner, with a mind of perfect joy, should give the lotus-hand, the sandals, and the yogi’s meditation belt.
You should not entertain any doubt in this matter; with a mind free from hesitation, reveal your own supreme and incomparable system of mantra practice.
With a mind free from doubt, do not harbor an inferior intellect regarding this; the supreme way of practicing secret mantra should be self-illuminated by yourself, peerless as you are.
By doing thus, you are grateful and a benefactor of the Buddhas;
and all those Vajradharas will protect you constantly.
By acting in this way, one repays the kindness shown to the Buddha; all those Vajra-holders as well will always provide protection for you in particular.
Your very self is the nature of wisdom and skillful means; like a supreme wish-fulfilling jewel, untiring and free from attachment, act now for the benefit of sentient beings.
Thus he should say:
"I am the nature of the activity of wisdom; being exalted like a wish-fulfilling jewel, and free from the doubt of non-arising, may you thus act for the benefit of sentient beings. So it is said.
Having prostrated, he should say:
"I shall do exactly as my lord commands."
"I shall do exactly as the Lord has commanded. Thus one should speak;
this is the procedure for granting permission (*anujñāvidhi*).
This is the ritual for bestowing the permission (*anujñā*).
Thereafter,
holding a parasol over his head, he should cause him to perform a circumambulation.
With palms joined in reverence, he should prostrate at the entrance of the mandala while holding a parasol, and say:
"This disciple who has been offered shall become a bearer of the tantra."

Having held a parasol over his head and caused him to circumambulate, one should join the palms at the entrance of the mandala and, together with the parasol, recite this binding: "This disciple, who has become a holder of the tantras, is now offered [to you]."
Having spoken thus, and having made such a request to the Lord of the Maṇḍala, one should set aside the parasol elsewhere and utter words that strike the heart of the disciple:
"Now you have become a Maṇḍala-ācārya, a holder of the mantras and tantras."
It is esteemed by the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the deities.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you should diligently draw the maṇḍala according to the prescribed rite, and practitioners should be engaged in accordance with the tantra.
Having seen and entered this supreme, most secret, and excellent maṇḍala,
you are today itself liberated from all sins and well-established.
There is no further falling away for you from this vehicle of great bliss;
the suffering of existence has ceased for you, so that you may achieve the ultimate transcendence of existence.
Today the Venerable One has been consecrated by all the Buddhas together with the Holders of the Thunderbolt;
it is certain that you are the sovereign in the great kingdom of the three realms.
There is no other evil in the three realms equal to dispassion;
therefore, you must never again practice the state of being free from desire for sensual pleasures.
"Enjoy all objects of desire, free from fear from any quarter;
the five meats and the nectar are to be consumed, O Rakṣasa, for this is the other commitment."
One should not commit the taking of life; one should not abandon a jewel of a woman;
one must not forsake one's teacher; the vow is difficult to transgress.
There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by a mind endowed with wisdom and skillful means;
do not fear, for you have no sin, according to the words of Vajrasattva.

VĀ: Thus, the word of the Tathāgata: "Now, you shall be the masters of the maṇḍala, upholders of the mantras and tantras; the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and even the gods will hold you in their thoughts. For the sake of compassion toward sentient beings, you must draw the maṇḍala with great effort according to the ritual procedures. You should apply yourselves to the mantras for the sake of practitioners; this is the most supreme and secret [teaching]."

By entering while beholding the maṇḍala, you are completely liberated from all sins. Today you abide in happiness; in this attainment of great bliss, there shall henceforth be no more death. You have transcended the suffering of existence; existence is now perfectly fulfilled. All the Buddhas, the Vajra-holders, have today appointed you as witnesses, O long-lived one.

The seventh is the vase-consecration (kalaśābhiṣeka), the eighth is the secret consecration (guhyābhiṣeka), and the ninth is from the wisdom-consecration (prajñābhiṣeka).
By means of the application of the reality-vajra (tattvavajra), one should bestow the vajra-vow (vajravratam) upon all.
The Teacher himself explains this sequence of the procedure for consecration.

Furthermore, from the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*: "The first is the water initiation; the second is the crown initiation; the third is the vajra initiation; the fourth is the master initiation; the fifth is the name initiation; the sixth is the perfect Buddha initiation; the seventh is the vase initiation; and the eighth is the secret initiation."

"Ninth is the wisdom empowerment; through the application of that very vajra, one bestows the universal vajra vow. The Teacher himself grants the prophecy. These are the stages of the supreme empowerments.
Thus it was said, and likewise stated in the *Dvikalparāja*:
The master, the secret, the wisdom, and the fourth, which is likewise.
In the second *Tattvaviniścaya-rāja* as well, it is said: "The master Guhyaprajñā and the fourth one are likewise."

In that regard, the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) is sixfold due to the distinctions among the water, crown, and vajra-lord preceptors (*ācārya*). This is because in all cases one is consecrated with vases by means of the vidyās such as Tathāgatalocanā and others. Since the preceptor’s consecration is to be bestowed through the supreme oral instruction (*upadeśa*), it involves a superior sprinkling; thus it is said that the vase consecration is the seventh. Because those five [consecrations], beginning with the water consecration, serve as the cause for the arising of that preceptor’s consecration, they too are called the "preceptor’s consecration. Therefore, everything is consistent.

The six initiations—the water, the crown, the vajra, the lord, the name, and the master—are the vase initiation, because in all cases one is consecrated by the vases of the Tathāgatas and the sequence of Locanā and the other goddesses.

It is said: "Because the master empowerment (ācāryābhiṣeka) is to be received as the most supreme and is accompanied by excellence, it is the seventh, namely the vase empowerment. Since that master empowerment is the cause from which [the others] arise, the five empowerments beginning with the water empowerment are also referred to as the master empowerment; therefore, there is no contradiction in all of them. This is the procedure for the empowerment of another.
Regarding the phrase "Empowering the Dependent Nature," this is the ritual for empowering the dependent nature.
